claims.label: Rules governing nature need not be those of traditional mathematics
claims.claim: Although theoretical science requires that the systems it studies follow definite rules, those rules need not be the equation-based rules of traditional mathematics; the more general rules embodied in simple computer programs are equally candidates for describing the natural world.
claims.quote: the crucial realization that led me to develop the new kind of science in this book is that there is in fact no reason to think that systems like those we see in nature should follow only such traditional mathematical rules.
claims.scope: rules underlying natural systems studied by the exact sciences
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Programs with very simple rules often behave in complex ways
claims.claim: When simple computer programs are enumerated and run systematically, their behavior is often far from simple, and some of the very simplest programs produce behavior as complex as any known.
claims.quote: despite the simplicity of their rules, the behavior of the programs was often far from simple. Indeed, even some of the very simplest programs that I looked at had behavior that was as complex as anything I had ever seen.
claims.scope: simple programs such as elementary cellular automata, enumerated systematically
measurable_quantities: fraction of rules in an enumerated class whose evolution from simple initial conditions is non-repetitive and non-nested
compressibility or entropy of the generated patterns
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive simulation of elementary and other small-rule cellular automata with Mathematica, Python or Golly, plus published enumerations of elementary cellular automaton behavior.

claims.label: Natural complexity arises because natural systems behave like typical programs
claims.claim: The great complexity seen across physical, biological and other natural systems is explained by those systems operating like typical simple programs, which commonly produce complex behavior, rather than by any special or supernatural source of complexity.
claims.quote: For all it takes is that systems in nature operate like typical programs and then it follows that their behavior will often be complex.
claims.scope: complex-looking physical, biological and other natural systems
measurable_quantities: whether observed complex natural patterns can be reproduced by minimal-rule programs
statistical similarity between natural patterns and outputs of simple programs
claims.candidate_data: Image and time-series collections of natural patterns (e.g. published shell-pattern image collections, snowflake image archives, turbulence data such as the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database) compared against simple-program simulations.

claims.label: Equation-based descriptions work for simple behavior but fail for complex behavior
claims.claim: Describing behavior with mathematical equations succeeds for fairly simple behavior such as planetary motion but almost inevitably fails when behavior is more complex, and descriptions based on natural selection share this limitation; thinking in terms of programs allows meaningful statements about highly complex behavior.
claims.quote: while their basic idea of describing behavior in terms of mathematical equations works well in cases like planetary motion where the behavior is fairly simple, it almost inevitably fails whenever the behavior is more complex.
claims.scope: traditional mathematical and evolutionary explanations in the existing sciences
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: The same basic forms of behavior recur in simple programs regardless of details
claims.claim: Across the world of simple programs the same basic forms of behavior occur repeatedly almost independently of the underlying details of the rules, suggesting universal principles of overall behavior that should also apply to systems throughout nature.
claims.quote: in the world of simple programs I have discovered that the same basic forms of behavior occur over and over again almost independent of underlying details.
claims.scope: simple programs of many types (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, etc.) and, by extension, natural systems
measurable_quantities: distribution of behavior classes (uniform, repetitive, nested, random-looking, localized structures) across different program types
robustness of that distribution to changes in rule representation
claims.candidate_data: Systematic enumeration of small cellular automata, Turing machines and other rule systems using public tools such as Mathematica or Python.

claims.label: Simple programs yield a straightforward explanation of thermodynamic behavior
claims.claim: The long-standing difficulty in understanding how thermodynamic behavior, including the Second Law of Thermodynamics, arises in physics can be resolved by a straightforward explanation drawn from the behavior of simple programs.
claims.quote: For more than a century, for example, there has been confusion about how thermodynamic behavior arises in physics. Yet from my discoveries about simple programs I have developed a quite straightforward explanation.
claims.scope: thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, specifically the basis of entropy increase
measurable_quantities: coarse-grained entropy over time in reversible simple-program models
agreement of such models with thermodynamic behavior of real gases
claims.candidate_data: Simulations of reversible cellular automata and lattice-gas models with public tools, compared with standard thermodynamic property data such as the NIST Chemistry WebBook.

claims.label: Universal computation is possible in systems with one-sentence rules
claims.claim: Contrary to the assumption that computational universality requires elaborate systems like electronic computers, there exist systems whose rules can be stated in a single sentence that are nevertheless universal, able to perform any possible computation.
claims.quote: there are systems whose rules are simple enough to describe in just one sentence that are nevertheless universal.
claims.scope: simple rule systems such as elementary cellular automata and small Turing machines
measurable_quantities: existence of a proof of universality for a specified simple-rule system
size of the rule (number of states, colors, cases)
claims.candidate_data: Published proofs and constructions in the computability literature, checkable by simulation with public tools.

claims.label: Most systems with non-simple behavior are computationally irreducible
claims.claim: Predicting a system's outcome by a mathematical shortcut is normally possible only for special systems with simple behavior; other systems are computationally irreducible, so their behavior can be found only by tracing each step with roughly as much computational effort as the system itself expends.
claims.quote: such systems are computationally irreducible—so that in effect the only way to find their behavior is to trace each of their steps, spending about as much computational effort as the systems themselves.
claims.scope: systems whose behavior is not obviously simple
measurable_quantities: existence or absence of predictive formulas or algorithms faster than direct simulation for specified systems
claims.candidate_data: Computational experiments searching for shortcuts in specific cellular automata, plus computational complexity theory results; no general dataset known.

claims.label: Computational irreducibility explains free will despite deterministic rules
claims.claim: Computational irreducibility provides an explanation of how humans, even if they follow definite underlying rules, can meaningfully be said to have free will.
claims.quote: it leads to an explanation of how we as humans—even though we may follow definite underlying rules—can still in a meaningful way show free will.
claims.scope: human behavior and the philosophical question of free will
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Complexity of simple abstract systems imposes fundamental limits on proof
claims.claim: The complexity found in simple abstract systems leads to fundamental limitations on mathematical proof, of the kind hinted at by Gödel's Theorem, and these limitations are relevant well beyond the narrow scope of current mathematics.
claims.quote: one of the consequences of this complexity is that it leads to fundamental limitations on the idea of proof that has been central to traditional mathematics.
claims.scope: mathematical proof applied to abstract systems based on simple programs
measurable_quantities: existence of undecidable or unprovable statements about specific simple systems
claims.candidate_data: Published undecidability results in logic and computability theory; no dataset known.

claims.label: Simple programs capture how genetic programs generate biological forms
claims.claim: Simple programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms and appear to capture essential mechanisms by which genetic programs generate observed biological forms, enabling new models and general abstract theories in biology.
claims.quote: such programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms—and for example seem to capture some of the essential mechanisms through which genetic programs manage to generate the actual biological forms we see.
claims.scope: biological morphogenesis and pigmentation patterns
measurable_quantities: fit between simple-program outputs and measured biological forms (shapes, pigment patterns, branching structures)
claims.candidate_data: Published shell-pattern image collections, plant morphology datasets and developmental-biology imaging data compared with simulated outputs.

claims.label: Sophisticated tasks need only extremely simple underlying rules
claims.claim: Contrary to engineering experience, performing sophisticated tasks does not require correspondingly complicated basic rules; extremely simple underlying rules, potentially implementable directly at the atomic scale, are often sufficient.
claims.quote: extremely simple underlying rules—that might for example potentially be implemented directly at the level of atoms—are often all that is needed.
claims.scope: technology and engineered systems, including nanotechnology
measurable_quantities: minimal rule complexity sufficient for specified computational or physical tasks
feasibility of atomic-scale implementations
claims.candidate_data: Results on minimal universal systems and molecular or DNA computing experiments in the published literature.

claims.label: Natural selection tends to oppose rather than generate complexity
claims.claim: Darwinian natural selection does not clearly imply the generation of complexity and in many respects tends to oppose it; a different mechanism, the intrinsic complexity of simple programs, is responsible for most great complexity in biology.
claims.quote: I will argue in this book that in many respects it tends to oppose complexity.
claims.scope: biological evolution and the origin of biological complexity
measurable_quantities: change in pattern complexity under simulated selection on simple-program genomes
comparison of complexity in selected versus unselected traits
claims.candidate_data: Artificial evolution simulations with public tools; comparative morphology data where available.

claims.label: A rule-90-type cellular automaton produces a nested self-similar pattern
claims.claim: A one-dimensional cellular automaton in which each cell becomes black when exactly one of its two neighbors was black (rule 90), started from a single black cell, produces an intricate but regular nested pattern made of triangular pieces that are smaller copies of the whole.
claims.quote: it actually consists of many nested triangular pieces that all have exactly the same form.
claims.scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 90 from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: self-similarity of the pattern
fractal dimension of the pattern
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of elementary cellular automata with public tools.

claims.label: Rule 30 from a single black cell produces an irregular, complex pattern
claims.claim: The elementary cellular automaton rule 30, started from a single black cell, produces a highly irregular and complex pattern with almost no overall regularity, rather than a uniform, repetitive or nested one.
claims.quote: Rather than getting a simple regular pattern as we might expect, the cellular automaton instead produces a pattern that seems extremely irregular and complex.
claims.scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 30 from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: compressibility of the pattern
presence or absence of periodicity or nesting
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 30 with public tools such as Mathematica, Python or Golly.

claims.label: Simple rules with simple initial conditions can yield highly complex behavior
claims.claim: As a general phenomenon, a system with simple underlying rules started from simple initial conditions can nevertheless show highly complex behavior.
claims.quote: even though the underlying rules for a system are simple, and even though the system is started from simple initial conditions, the behavior that the system shows can nevertheless be highly complex.
claims.scope: simple programs and other systems with simple rules and simple initial conditions
measurable_quantities: complexity measures of output as a function of rule and initial-condition size
claims.candidate_data: Systematic simulation of enumerated simple programs with public tools.

claims.label: Complexity from simple rules accounts for most complexity in nature
claims.claim: The generation of complex behavior from simple rules and simple initial conditions is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity seen in nature.
claims.quote: I will argue that it is this basic phenomenon that is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity that we see in nature.
claims.scope: complex phenomena throughout the natural world
measurable_quantities: proportion of well-studied complex natural phenomena successfully modeled by simple deterministic rules versus random inputs or complex mechanisms
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Rule 30's center column shows no deviation from randomness over a million steps
claims.claim: The sequence of cell colors directly below the initial black cell in rule 30 does not repeat in its first million steps, and statistical tests show no meaningful deviation from perfect randomness.
claims.quote: in the first million steps in this sequence, for example, it never repeats, and indeed none of the tests I have ever done on it show any meaningful deviation at all from perfect randomness.
claims.scope: center column of elementary cellular automaton rule 30 from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: period of the center-column sequence
results of standard randomness test batteries
frequency of black versus white cells
claims.candidate_data: Direct computation of the rule 30 center column (also listed in OEIS) tested with the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite or TestU01.

claims.label: Some cellular automata make even average properties hard to predict
claims.claim: Some simple cellular automata, such as rule 110, are more complex than random-looking ones like rule 30: they mix regular regions with interacting localized structures, so that even average properties of their behavior become very difficult to predict.
claims.quote: there are cellular automata whose behavior is in effect still more complex—and in which even such averages become very difficult to predict.
claims.scope: elementary cellular automata with localized structures, especially rule 110
measurable_quantities: density of black cells over time
number and types of localized structures
variance of averages across runs
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 110 with public tools.

claims.label: Rule 110's fate can be determined only by running it
claims.claim: Whether the localized structures in rule 110 eventually annihilate into a regular pattern or proliferate into randomness apparently cannot be determined in advance; the only reliable method is to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as needed.
claims.quote: The only sure way to answer these questions, it seems, is just to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as are needed
claims.scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 110 and similar systems
measurable_quantities: existence of any predictive shortcut for rule 110 evolution faster than direct simulation
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 110 and computational-complexity results on cellular automaton prediction.

claims.section: The Need for a New Intuition
claims.label: Rule 110 from one black cell becomes periodic with period 240 after about 2780 steps
claims.claim: Rule 110 started from a single black cell resolves after about 2780 steps: one localized structure survives and interacts with periodic stripes from the left to give behavior that repeats every 240 steps.
claims.quote: the outcome is finally clear after about 2780 steps: one structure survives, and that structure interacts with the periodic stripes coming from the left to produce behavior that repeats every 240 steps.
claims.scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 110 from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: step at which the right-hand region becomes periodic
period of the eventual behavior
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 110 with public tools.

claims.section: The Need for a New Intuition
claims.label: Identical cell rules yield diverse behaviors through different configurations
claims.claim: Even though every cell of a cellular automaton follows the same rule, different configurations of cell colors can collectively produce many different kinds of behavior, such as regular backgrounds and distinct localized structures.
claims.quote: even though individual cells follow the same rule, different configurations of cells with different sequences of colors can together produce all sorts of different kinds of behavior.
claims.scope: cellular automata, exemplified by rule 110
measurable_quantities: catalog of distinct localized structures and background patterns produced by one rule
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 110 and published catalogs of its localized structures.

claims.section: The Need for a New Intuition
claims.label: Intuition that complex results need complex plans comes from engineering
claims.claim: The intuition that complex objects require complex construction plans fails because it derives from engineering, where designers restrict themselves to systems whose behavior they can understand and predict, a constraint nature does not share.
claims.quote: Yet to do this reliably, we have to restrict ourselves to systems whose behavior we can readily understand and predict—for unless we can foresee how a system will behave, we cannot be sure that the system will do what we want.
claims.scope: human intuition about complexity and the practice of engineering
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: The Need for a New Intuition
claims.label: Systems with simple rules and complex behavior are very common in nature
claims.claim: Because nature is not constrained to predictable designs, systems whose simple rules produce complex behavior, like rule 30 and rule 110, are very common in nature.
claims.quote: one of the important conclusions of this book is that such systems are actually very common in nature.
claims.scope: natural systems generally
measurable_quantities: frequency with which complex natural phenomena are well modeled by simple-rule systems
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before
claims.label: Complex cellular-automaton-like patterns are absent from historical ornament
claims.claim: Historical ornamental art contains many repetitive patterns and some nested ones, but the more complicated patterns produced by simple cellular automata such as rule 30 never appear to have been used.
claims.quote: Repetitive patterns are common and some nested patterns are seen, but the more complicated kinds of patterns discussed in this chapter do not ever appear to have been used.
claims.scope: historical ornamental art across cultures
measurable_quantities: occurrence of non-repetitive, non-nested rule-based patterns in catalogued historical ornament
claims.candidate_data: Museum collection databases with ornament images (e.g. the Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access collection) and published pattern catalogs.

claims.section: Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before
claims.label: Computers enable discoveries beyond working out mathematical equations
claims.claim: Computers are not limited to computing the consequences of mathematical equations; directly studying the behavior of even the simplest computer programs yields fundamental scientific discoveries.
claims.quote: computers are not just limited to working out consequences of mathematical equations. And indeed, what we have seen in this chapter is that there are fundamental discoveries that can be made if one just studies directly the behavior of even some of the very simplest computer programs.
claims.scope: the role of computers in basic science
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before
claims.label: Unknown phenomena are found only by systematic, preconception-free experiments
claims.claim: Phenomena not already known to exist can be found only by very systematic and general experiments whose results are examined with as few preconceptions as possible.
claims.quote: the only way to find phenomena that one does not already know exist is to do very systematic and general experiments, and then to look at the results with as few preconceptions as possible.
claims.scope: scientific methodology, especially computer experiments
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before
claims.label: Lack of adequate computers delayed discovery of complexity from simple rules
claims.claim: A main reason that complexity from simple programs was not discovered before the 1980s is that computer technology powerful enough for the required large-scale exploratory experiments did not yet exist, together with a lack of intuition drawn from practical computing.
claims.quote: one of the main reasons that the discoveries I describe in this chapter were not made before the 1980s is just that computer technology did not yet exist powerful enough to do the kinds of exploratory experiments that were needed.
claims.scope: history of science and computing
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before
claims.label: It is usually very hard to foresee what even a simple program will do
claims.claim: Practical computing shows that it is usually very difficult to foresee the behavior of even a simple program, which is why software bugs are so common; the simple structure of cellular automaton rules likewise does not make their behavior easy to predict.
claims.quote: from experience in practical computing one knows that it is usually very difficult to foresee what even a simple program will do.
claims.scope: simple programs, including software and cellular automata
measurable_quantities: success rate of predicting program outputs without execution
bug rates relative to program size
claims.candidate_data: Public software defect datasets (e.g. Defects4J) and program-comprehension studies in the software engineering literature.

claims.section: Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before
claims.label: Primes follow simple generating rules yet are distributed seemingly randomly
claims.claim: The prime numbers, though generated by simple rules, have a distribution that seems in many respects random, an early instance of complexity from simple rules that mathematics largely neglected in favor of proving regularities.
claims.quote: The rules for generating primes are simple, yet their distribution seems in many respects random.
claims.scope: distribution of prime numbers
measurable_quantities: statistics of prime gaps
deviations of prime counts from smooth approximations
claims.candidate_data: Prime tables and prime-gap sequences in the OEIS and public prime databases, analyzed with standard number-theory software.

claims.section: Why These Discoveries Were Not Made Before
claims.label: Complexity from simple programs was never discovered before despite many hints
claims.claim: Although there were many hints over several centuries, including primes, digits of pi, iterated maps and the Game of Life, the basic phenomenon of simple programs producing complex behavior was never identified before Wolfram's work.
claims.quote: despite many hints over the course of several centuries, the basic phenomenon that I have described in this chapter was never discovered before.
claims.scope: history of science and mathematics
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Overall behavior types are similar across all kinds of simple programs
claims.claim: Whatever kind of underlying rules a simple program uses (cellular automata, mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, register machines, symbolic systems), the overall behavior that emerges falls into the same few basic types first seen in elementary cellular automata.
claims.quote: whatever kind of underlying rules one uses, the behavior that emerges turns out to be remarkably similar to the basic examples that we have already seen in cellular automata.
claims.scope: simple programs of all the kinds surveyed in chapter 3
measurable_quantities: classification of behavior (repetitive, nested, random, localized structures) across exhaustive or sampled rule spaces of each system type
claims.candidate_data: Can be checked computationally by enumerating small rule spaces of each system type with public tools such as the Wolfram Language or open-source simulators.

claims.label: Most elementary cellular automata give fixed-size patterns from a single black cell
claims.claim: Among the 256 elementary (two-color, nearest-neighbor) cellular automata started from a single black cell, about two-thirds produce patterns that stay of fixed size and about one-third produce patterns that grow forever, with about 14% yielding patterns more complicated than repetition.
claims.quote: In about two-thirds of all the cellular automata shown on the last few pages [54, 55, 56], the patterns produced remain of a fixed size. But in about one-third of cases, the patterns instead grow forever.
claims.scope: the 256 elementary cellular automata, single-black-cell initial condition
measurable_quantities: fraction of rules with bounded pattern width
fraction with growing patterns
fraction with non-repetitive growing patterns
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by simulating all 256 elementary rules, e.g. with the Wolfram Language CellularAutomaton function or any open-source elementary CA simulator.

claims.label: Ten of the 256 elementary cellular automata produce apparent randomness
claims.claim: Of the 256 elementary cellular automata started from a single black cell, 10 produce patterns that seem in many respects random, falling into three basic forms, while 24 produce nested patterns falling into only three fundamentally different forms.
claims.quote: And out of the 256 rules discussed here, it turns out that 10 yield such apparent randomness. There are three basic forms, as illustrated on the facing page.
claims.scope: the 256 elementary cellular automata, single-black-cell initial condition
measurable_quantities: number of rules with random-looking patterns
number of rules with nested patterns
number of inequivalent forms of each
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by simulating all 256 elementary rules and applying randomness or compression measures to the resulting patterns.

claims.label: Beyond a threshold, more complex rules do not give more complex behavior
claims.claim: At least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules of a system does not lead to more complex overall behavior; in cellular automata, all the ingredients for the most complex behavior already exist in the elementary two-color rules.
claims.quote: at least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules for a system does not ultimately lead to more complex overall behavior.
claims.scope: simple programs generally, illustrated by cellular automata with more colors
measurable_quantities: complexity measures (e.g. compressibility, entropy) of behavior as a function of rule size
claims.candidate_data: Can be probed computationally by sampling cellular automata with increasing numbers of colors or neighbors and comparing behavior-complexity measures.

claims.label: About 85% of three-color totalistic cellular automata behave regularly
claims.claim: About 85% of the 2187 three-color nearest-neighbor totalistic cellular automata produce behavior that is ultimately quite regular, while the remainder include rules with seemingly random behavior and rules with interacting localized structures like rule 110.
claims.quote: About 85% of all three-color totalistic cellular automata produce behavior that is ultimately quite regular.
claims.scope: three-color nearest-neighbor totalistic cellular automata from a single gray cell
measurable_quantities: fraction of the 2187 rules with ultimately repetitive or nested behavior
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by simulating all 2187 three-color totalistic rules with the Wolfram Language or an open-source CA simulator.

claims.label: No basic mobile automaton shows behavior beyond repetition or nesting
claims.claim: None of the 65,536 two-color mobile automata whose rule updates only the active cell shows behavior more complex than repetition or nesting; complex behavior appears only when the rule can also update the active cell's neighbors, and even then it is rare.
claims.quote: Of the 65,536 possible mobile automata with rules of the kind discussed so far it turns out that not a single one shows more complex behavior.
claims.scope: two-color mobile automata with a single active cell
measurable_quantities: behavior class of each of the 65,536 rules
fraction of extended (4,294,967,296) rules with nested or random behavior
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by exhaustive simulation of the 65,536 rules and random sampling of the extended rule space.

claims.label: Complex behavior correlates with many cells being active at once
claims.claim: In generalized mobile automata, complex behavior almost never occurs unless many cells are active simultaneously, and this correlation between overall activity and complexity helps explain why complexity is much more common in cellular automata than in mobile automata.
claims.quote: complex behavior almost never occurs except when large numbers of cells are active at the same time.
claims.scope: mobile automata, generalized mobile automata and cellular automata
measurable_quantities: number of active cells over time
behavior complexity per rule
correlation between the two across sampled rules
claims.candidate_data: Computable by sampling generalized mobile automaton rules and measuring activity and pattern complexity.

claims.label: Two- and three-state two-color Turing machines give only repetition or nesting
claims.claim: All 4096 two-state, two-color Turing machines, and all of the roughly three million three-state, two-color Turing machines started on a blank tape, ultimately produce only repetitive or nested patterns.
claims.quote: all ultimately turn out to yield just repetitive or nested patterns—at least if they are started with all cells white.
claims.scope: two-color Turing machines with two or three head states, blank initial tape
measurable_quantities: behavior class of every machine in the enumerated rule spaces
claims.candidate_data: Computable by exhaustive enumeration of small Turing machines, as in published busy-beaver and small-Turing-machine enumeration work.

claims.label: Four head states suffice for random-looking Turing machine behavior
claims.claim: Two-color Turing machines with four head states can produce seemingly random behavior (about five in every million such rules), and allowing more than four states makes apparent randomness only slightly more common without changing the kinds of behavior seen.
claims.quote: With four states, however, more complicated behavior immediately becomes possible. Indeed, in about five out of every million rules of this kind, one gets patterns with features that seem in many respects random
claims.scope: two-color Turing machines with four or more head states, blank initial tape
measurable_quantities: fraction of four-state machines with random-looking patterns
same fraction for five or more states
claims.candidate_data: Computable by random sampling of four- and five-state Turing machines with public simulation tools.

claims.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only produce nested patterns
claims.claim: Substitution systems in which each element is replaced according to its own color alone always produce nested patterns, so obtaining behavior more complicated than nesting requires rules that depend on at least one neighboring element.
claims.quote: To get behavior that is more complicated than simple nesting, it follows therefore that one must consider substitution systems whose rules depend not only on the color of a single element, but also on the color of at least one of its neighbors.
claims.scope: parallel substitution systems
claims.candidate_data: Settled by the standard theory of morphic and automatic sequences, and checkable by simulation.

claims.label: Substitution systems with deletion need three or more colors for complexity
claims.claim: Among two-color substitution systems that allow elements to be destroyed, those with slow growth produce only simple repetitive patterns, but allowing three or four colors immediately makes patterns as random-looking as those of cellular automata possible.
claims.quote: allowing elements to have three or four colors rather than just two immediately makes much more complicated behavior possible.
claims.scope: neighbor-dependent substitution systems with creation and destruction of elements
measurable_quantities: behavior class of slow-growth rules with two, three and four colors
claims.candidate_data: Computable by enumerating or sampling such substitution rules in the Wolfram Language or similar tools.

claims.label: Text-editor-like search-and-replace rules can generate great complexity
claims.claim: Sequential substitution systems, which repeatedly apply the first matching search-and-replace rule like a text editor, give only simple behavior with two replacements and two elements, but with three replacements about one in 10,000 random rules produces seemingly random behavior.
claims.quote: just by using the simple operations available even in a very basic text editor, it is still ultimately possible to produce behavior of great complexity.
claims.scope: sequential substitution (string rewriting) systems
measurable_quantities: fraction of sampled three-replacement rules with random-looking growth
claims.candidate_data: Computable by sampling string-rewriting rules with the Wolfram Language or any string-processing environment.

claims.label: One-element-deletion tag systems reduce to neighbor-independent substitution
claims.claim: A tag system that removes only one element per step always acts as a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system and so produces only repetitive or nested patterns, whereas removing two elements per step can yield very complicated behavior.
claims.quote: if only one element is removed at each step, then a tag system always effectively acts just like a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system of the kind we discussed on page 83.
claims.scope: tag systems
claims.candidate_data: Provable directly from the definitions and checkable by simulating small tag systems.

claims.label: Simple cyclic tag systems show random fluctuations in sequence growth
claims.claim: Some cyclic tag systems with two alternating blocks, started from a single black element, produce sequences whose average growth is steady but whose fluctuations about that growth are in many respects random.
claims.quote: if one looks at the fluctuations in this growth, as in the plots on the next page, then one finds that these fluctuations are in many respects random.
claims.scope: cyclic tag systems with two blocks
measurable_quantities: sequence length versus step
statistical randomness of deviations from mean growth
claims.candidate_data: Computable by simulating cyclic tag systems and applying standard randomness tests to the length fluctuations.

claims.label: Register machines need eight instructions to show complex behavior
claims.claim: Among two-register machines with increment and decrement-jump instructions, all programs of up to four instructions behave repetitively, only two five-instruction programs give nesting, none up to seven instructions is substantially more complicated, and 126 of the 11,019,960,576 eight-instruction programs show complex behavior.
claims.quote: But with eight instructions, 126 out of the 11,019,960,576 possible programs finally do show more complicated behavior.
claims.scope: two-register machines with increment and decrement-jump instructions
measurable_quantities: behavior class of every program of length 1 to 8
claims.candidate_data: Computable by exhaustive enumeration of register machine programs, which is feasible though large at length eight.

claims.label: Short programs in ordinary low-level languages can behave randomly
claims.claim: Because register machines idealize programs in low-level languages such as C, Basic, Java or assembler, searching many millions of short programs in such languages typically yields at least a few with complex, seemingly random behavior.
claims.quote: searching through many millions of short programs typically yields at least a few that exhibit complex and seemingly random behavior.
claims.scope: short programs in practical low-level programming languages
measurable_quantities: fraction of enumerated short programs with random-looking output or register traces
claims.candidate_data: Could be tested by enumerating short programs in a small language or instruction set and analyzing their traces; no standard corpus is known.

claims.label: Combinator-like symbolic rewriting systems can behave randomly
claims.claim: Symbolic systems that repeatedly apply a single rewrite rule of the form e[x_][y_] → (expression in x and y) to nested expressions can, like other simple programs, produce behavior that is complex and seemingly random rather than stabilizing.
claims.quote: But often—just as in so many other kinds of systems—the behavior is instead complex and seemingly quite random.
claims.scope: combinator-like symbolic expression rewriting systems
measurable_quantities: expression size versus step
randomness of size differences
claims.candidate_data: Computable using the Wolfram Language ReplaceAll operation or any term-rewriting system.

claims.label: Complexity does not depend on the special features of cellular automata
claims.claim: Removing the special features of cellular automata, such as a rigid array of cells and parallel updating, does not prevent complex behavior from simple rules, so the phenomenon of complexity is universal and independent of the details of particular systems.
claims.quote: So this suggests that in fact the phenomenon of complexity is quite universal—and quite independent of the details of particular systems.
claims.scope: all kinds of simple programs
measurable_quantities: existence of complex behavior in each system class with simple rules
claims.candidate_data: Partly checkable computationally by surveying rule spaces of many system types.

claims.label: The rule-complexity threshold for complex behavior is very low
claims.claim: Systems with sufficiently simple rules show only repetition, slightly more complicated rules often add nesting, and complex behavior requires crossing a threshold in rule complexity, but in every kind of system studied this threshold is extremely low.
claims.quote: The remarkable discovery that we have made, however, is that this threshold is typically extremely low.
claims.scope: all kinds of simple programs
measurable_quantities: smallest rule size at which repetition, nesting and random-looking behavior first appear in each system class
claims.candidate_data: Computable by exhaustive enumeration of the smallest rules in each system class.

claims.label: Repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures dominate everywhere
claims.claim: The four themes of repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures are the dominant types of behavior across a vast range of systems, and these overall behavior types are almost independent of the details of the underlying rules.
claims.quote: the basic themes of repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures that we already saw in specific cellular automata in the previous chapter are actually very general, and in fact represent the dominant themes in the behavior of a vast range of different systems.
claims.scope: simple programs and, by extension, a vast range of systems
measurable_quantities: distribution of behavior classes across rule spaces
claims.candidate_data: Partly checkable computationally; no agreed automatic classifier of the four themes is known.

claims.section: How the Discoveries in This Chapter Were Made
claims.label: Overall behavior of natural systems can be inferred without knowing their details
claims.claim: Because the typical types of behavior are independent of rule details, one can make fundamental statements about the overall behavior of a natural system without knowing its internal details, and its important features will usually be ones already seen in very simple programs.
claims.quote: even if we do not know all the details of what is inside some specific system in nature, we can still potentially make fundamental statements about its overall behavior.
claims.scope: systems in nature
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: How the Discoveries in This Chapter Were Made
claims.label: Computer experiments let one discover phenomena not anticipated in advance
claims.claim: A methodology based on computer experiments, in which one runs precisely specified programs and observes their behavior, can discover genuinely unexpected phenomena that a traditional approach of constructing examples of predefined behavior would miss, while giving results as precise as mathematical statements.
claims.quote: And the great advantage of such an experimental approach is that it does not require one to know in advance exactly what kinds of behavior can occur.
claims.scope: methodology of studying simple programs
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: How the Discoveries in This Chapter Were Made
claims.label: One can never start a computer experiment with too simple a system
claims.claim: Computer experiments should study the simplest possible systems with the simplest possible procedures, because simple systems already show complex behavior, and the most common mistake is studying systems far more complicated than necessary.
claims.quote: in my experience the single most common mistake in doing computer experiments is to look at systems that are vastly more complicated than is necessary.
claims.scope: design of computer experiments
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Number systems fully solvable by analysis show only simple behavior
claims.claim: Systems based on numbers that traditional mathematics (e.g. calculus) can analyze completely end up showing only fairly simple behavior; textbook systems are selected for analyzability and therefore are simple.
claims.quote: Inevitably, however, when such complete analysis is possible, the final behavior that is found is fairly simple.
claims.scope: number-based systems treated in traditional science and mathematics
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Simple arithmetic systems can produce highly complex behavior
claims.claim: When systems based on numbers are studied by computer experiment rather than by mathematical analysis, even very simple ones turn out to produce highly complex behavior.
claims.quote: if one ignores the need for analysis and instead just looks at the results of computer experiments, then one quickly finds that even rather simple systems based on numbers can lead to highly complex behavior.
claims.scope: simple iterative systems defined by arithmetic operations on numbers
measurable_quantities: digit-sequence patterns of iterated values
statistical randomness of iterated values
presence or absence of repetition
claims.candidate_data: Reproducible by direct computation in any arbitrary-precision arithmetic environment; integer sequences in the OEIS.

claims.label: Base-2 digits of powers of 3 look random beyond small-scale structure
claims.claim: Successive powers of 3 written in base 2 form a pattern that, apart from some small-scale structure, appears random for all practical purposes, even though it comes from repeated multiplication by 3.
claims.quote: Some small-scale structure is visible, but on a larger scale the pattern seems for all practical purposes random.
claims.scope: base-2 digit sequences of powers of 3
measurable_quantities: statistical randomness tests on base-2 digits of 3^n
frequency of digit blocks
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic; OEIS lists powers of 3.

claims.label: Fractional parts of powers of 3/2 are complex and apparently random
claims.claim: The fractional parts of successive powers of 3/2, a base-independent measure of size, show the same complexity and apparent randomness that appears in their digit sequences.
claims.quote: they too exhibit the kind of complexity and apparent randomness that is evident at the level of digits.
claims.scope: fractional parts of (3/2)^n
measurable_quantities: distribution of fractional parts of (3/2)^n
correlations between successive values
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with exact rational arithmetic; there is extensive number-theory literature on the distribution of (3/2)^n mod 1.

claims.label: Simple whole-number rules can yield complex sizes, not just complex digits
claims.claim: Simple rules acting only on whole numbers (such as multiplying by 5/2 when even and adding 1 then halving when odd) can produce sequences whose overall sizes fluctuate in a complex, apparently random way with no sign of repetition, so complexity is not just an artifact of looking at digits.
claims.quote: So even if one just looks at overall sizes of whole numbers it is still possible to get great complexity in systems based on numbers.
claims.scope: simple piecewise arithmetic maps on whole numbers
measurable_quantities: sizes of iterated values over millions of steps
detection of eventual periodicity
statistics of size fluctuations
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic.

claims.label: Non-local arithmetic rules still behave like local cellular automata
claims.claim: Although arithmetic operations are non-local in digits (carries can propagate arbitrarily far) while cellular automaton rules are local, the overall behavior of number-based systems is very similar to that of cellular automata, so the details of underlying rules do not crucially affect the kinds of behavior that occur.
claims.quote: But despite fundamental differences like this in underlying rules, the overall behavior produced by systems based on numbers is still very similar to what one sees for example in cellular automata.
claims.scope: number-based systems compared with cellular automata and other simple programs
measurable_quantities: classification of behavior types (repetitive, nested, random, localized structures) across rule families
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating simple arithmetic and cellular automaton rules.

claims.label: Reverse-and-add in base 2 shows localized structures and never repeats
claims.claim: The base-2 reverse-and-add process (add a number to its digit-reversal) started from 512 produces localized structures like those in cellular automata, and its overall pattern never appears to become simply repetitive.
claims.quote: Localized structures are visible, but the overall pattern never seems to take on any kind of simple repetitive form.
claims.scope: base-2 reverse-and-add iteration from particular starting numbers
measurable_quantities: digit patterns over millions of steps
detection of eventual periodic structure
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic; OEIS contains base-2 reverse-and-add trajectories.

claims.label: Recursive sequences using only addition and subtraction can be complex
claims.claim: Recursive integer sequences whose rule refers back a variable distance (e.g. f[n - f[n - 1]]) and uses only addition and subtraction can produce fluctuations that are complex and in many respects random.
claims.quote: even though the rules ultimately involve only addition and subtraction, they nevertheless correspond to programs that are capable of producing behavior of great complexity.
claims.scope: nested recursive integer sequences (Hofstadter-like sequences)
measurable_quantities: fluctuations of f[n] about its trend
balance of positive and negative fluctuations
correlation with base-2 digits of n
claims.candidate_data: OEIS entries for Hofstadter-type meta-Fibonacci sequences, and direct computation.

claims.label: The sequence of primes is in many respects random
claims.claim: Even though the primes are generated by a simple sieving rule, the sequence of primes appears in many respects remarkably random.
claims.quote: the actual sequence of primes that is obtained seems in many respects remarkably random.
claims.scope: the sequence of prime numbers
measurable_quantities: prime gaps
deviations of prime counts from Li(x)
parity of number of primes below n
randomness tests on prime indicator sequence
claims.candidate_data: OEIS prime sequences and gap records, published prime tables, and fast sieving software such as primesieve.

claims.label: Complexity in number-theoretic sequences arises from their generating rules
claims.claim: Sequences defined by simple properties of numbers (primes, divisor sums, representations as sums of squares or primes) show complexity that persists despite centuries of number theory, and this complexity arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules generating them, just as in other simple programs.
claims.quote: such sequences of numbers exhibit complexity that somehow arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules by which the sequences are generated.
claims.scope: integer sequences defined by simple number-theoretic properties
measurable_quantities: randomness statistics of divisor-function and representation-count sequences
claims.candidate_data: OEIS entries for divisor sums, sum-of-squares counts and Goldbach partition counts.

claims.label: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes
claims.claim: Despite pi's simple definition, its digit sequence shows no significant regularity in all computed digits and appears for practical purposes completely random.
claims.quote: Despite the simplicity of its definition, the digit sequence of π seems for practical purposes completely random.
claims.scope: digit sequence of pi in any base
measurable_quantities: digit and block frequencies of pi
statistical randomness test results on pi's digits
claims.candidate_data: Published large-scale computations of pi's digits (trillions of digits) and statistical normality analyses of them.

claims.label: Square roots of non-square integers have random-looking digits
claims.claim: As far as can be determined, the square root of every whole number that is not a perfect square has a digit sequence that appears completely random.
claims.quote: so far as one can tell, all whole numbers other than perfect squares have square roots whose digit sequences appear completely random.
claims.scope: digit sequences of square roots of non-square integers
measurable_quantities: digit and block frequencies of square roots
statistical randomness tests on their digits
claims.candidate_data: Published high-precision digit computations of sqrt(2) and other square roots, and direct computation.

claims.label: Cube roots, logarithms and exponentials also have random-looking digits
claims.claim: Beyond square roots, almost all cube roots, fourth roots, logarithms and exponentials of simple numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
claims.quote: And so far as one can tell, almost all these kinds of numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
claims.scope: digit sequences of higher roots, logarithms and exponentials of small integers
measurable_quantities: digit and block frequencies
statistical randomness tests on digit expansions
claims.candidate_data: Published high-precision computations of constants such as e, log 2 and cube roots, and direct computation.

claims.label: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences
claims.claim: Every rational number p/q has a digit sequence that eventually repeats (with period at most q - 1), and rational numbers are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences.
claims.quote: In fact, rational numbers turn out to be the only kinds of numbers that have repetitive digit sequences.
claims.scope: digit expansions of real numbers
claims.candidate_data: Standard proofs in elementary number theory.

claims.label: Roots never have nested digit sequences
claims.claim: Nested digit sequences, such as those produced by substitution systems, never correspond to numbers obtainable by taking roots (square roots, cube roots, and so on).
claims.quote: such a digit sequence never corresponds to a number that can be obtained by the mathematical operation of taking roots.
claims.scope: digit expansions of algebraic numbers obtained as roots
claims.candidate_data: Published transcendence results on automatic (substitution-generated) numbers in the number-theory literature.

claims.label: Continued fractions of pi and higher roots look random
claims.claim: In continued fraction representation, square roots are purely repetitive and e shows definite regularity, but pi, cube roots, fourth roots and similar numbers have continued fraction terms that seem essentially random.
claims.quote: But for π, as well as for cube roots, fourth roots, and so on, the continued fraction representations one gets seem essentially random.
claims.scope: continued fraction expansions of common irrational numbers
measurable_quantities: distribution of continued fraction terms compared with the Gauss–Kuzmin distribution
periodicity of terms
claims.candidate_data: OEIS entries for continued fraction terms of pi, cube roots and e, and direct computation.

claims.label: Numbers from simple operations are intrinsically complex in any representation
claims.claim: For any representation of numbers in which recovering the value takes comparable effort for all numbers, some numbers look simple but others produced by simple mathematical operations look random, so such numbers are often intrinsically complex independent of representation.
claims.quote: numbers generated by simple mathematical operations are often in some intrinsic sense complex, independent of the particular representation that one uses to look at them.
claims.scope: numbers generated by simple mathematical operations, across number representations
measurable_quantities: apparent randomness of the same numbers across digit, continued-fraction and other representations
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable for standard representations; none known for a general test.

claims.label: Axis crossings of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] follow a continued-fraction substitution system
claims.claim: For a sum of two sine functions Sin[x] + Sin[a x], the arrangement of axis crossings is generated by a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from successive continued fraction terms of (a - 1)/(a + 1), giving nested patterns when a is a quadratic irrational.
claims.quote: for any curve like Sin[x] + Sin[α x] the relative arrangements of these crossing points turn out to be related to the output of a generalized substitution system in which the rule at each step is obtained from a term in the continued fraction representation of (α - 1)/(α + 1).
claims.scope: zero sets of sums of two sinusoids
measurable_quantities: positions of zeros of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] compared with substitution-system output
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable numerically; related results in the literature on Sturmian sequences.

claims.section: Iterated Maps and the Chaos Phenomenon
claims.label: The shift map only transcribes randomness from its initial condition
claims.claim: The shift map (doubling modulo 1) generates no randomness of its own: it just moves digits of the initial number leftward, so its output is random only if the initial number's digit sequence was already random.
claims.quote: in no real sense is any randomness actually being generated by the evolution of this system. Instead, it is just that randomness that was inserted in the digit sequence of the original number shows up in the results one gets.
claims.scope: the shift map and similar chaotic maps that act as digit shifts
measurable_quantities: outputs of the shift map from initial conditions with simple versus random digit sequences
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with exact rational or arbitrary-precision arithmetic.

claims.section: Iterated Maps and the Chaos Phenomenon
claims.label: Some simple iterated maps generate randomness intrinsically from simple seeds
claims.claim: Some simple iterated maps, such as taking the fractional part of 3x/2, produce behavior that looks random even when started from very simple initial numbers like 1/2, so they intrinsically generate randomness rather than transcribing it from initial conditions.
claims.quote: a crucial discovery in this book is that systems like (a) and (b) on pages 150 and 151 can show behavior that seems in many respects random even when their initial conditions show no sign of randomness and are in fact extremely simple.
claims.scope: simple one-dimensional iterated maps on [0, 1]
measurable_quantities: randomness statistics of iterates from rational initial conditions
digit-sequence complexity of iterates
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with exact rational arithmetic.

claims.label: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not itself produce randomness
claims.claim: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (the chaos phenomenon) only amplifies differences already present in initial conditions, so on its own it contributes nothing to the ultimate production of randomness, even in systems that also show intrinsic randomness.
claims.quote: this phenomenon on its own can make no contribution at all to what we can reasonably consider the ultimate production of randomness.
claims.scope: chaotic dynamical systems and iterated maps
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Continuous cellular automata show the same complexity as discrete ones
claims.claim: Cellular automata whose cells take a continuous range of gray levels, updated by simple maps of the neighborhood average, show the same kind of complexity as ordinary discrete cellular automata, and can even show localized structures.
claims.quote: despite the presence of continuous gray levels, the behavior that is produced exhibits the same kind of complexity that we have seen in many ordinary cellular automata and other systems with discrete underlying elements.
claims.scope: one-dimensional continuous-valued cellular automata
measurable_quantities: spatial-temporal patterns of gray levels
randomness statistics
presence of localized structures
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with exact or high-precision arithmetic.

claims.label: Nature does not fundamentally follow continuous differential equations
claims.claim: Although almost all traditional models in physics (Maxwell, Einstein, Schrödinger equations) are partial differential equations, nature does not fundamentally follow these continuous mathematical abstractions.
claims.quote: it is certainly not that nature fundamentally follows these abstractions.
claims.scope: fundamental laws of physics
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Partial differential equations predominate largely by historical accident
claims.claim: The dominance of partial differential equations as models in science is in many respects a historical accident of their being solvable by explicit formulas before computers; had computers come earlier, scientific modeling would probably be very different.
claims.quote: I suspect that in fact the current predominance of partial differential equations is in many respects a historical accident—and that had computer technology been developed earlier in the history of mathematics, the situation would probably now be very different.
claims.scope: history of mathematical modeling in physics and other sciences
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Simple partial differential equations can show complex behavior
claims.claim: Complex behavior of the kind seen in simple programs is not restricted to discrete systems: some fairly simple partial differential equations, found by searching, produce highly complex patterns, even with apparently discrete patches.
claims.quote: we now know that the same kind of behavior can also occur in completely continuous systems such as partial differential equations.
claims.scope: one-dimensional nonlinear partial differential equations
measurable_quantities: numerical solutions of the equations
robustness of patterns across numerical schemes and resolutions
claims.candidate_data: Reproducible by numerical PDE solvers.

claims.label: Complexity is not rarer in continuous systems, only harder to detect
claims.claim: Complexity is probably not fundamentally rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones; it was much easier to discover in discrete systems because they can be studied directly by computer experiment without approximation artifacts.
claims.quote: Probably complexity is not in any fundamental sense rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones. But the point is that discrete systems can typically be investigated in a much more direct way than continuous ones.
claims.scope: continuous versus discrete dynamical systems
measurable_quantities: fraction of sampled rules showing complex behavior in continuous versus discrete rule spaces
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Phenomena seen in discrete simple programs also occur in simple continuous systems
claims.claim: Essentially all of the phenomena observed in discrete simple programs can also be found in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
claims.quote: I suspect that essentially all of the various phenomena that we have observed in discrete systems in the past several chapters can in fact also be found even in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
claims.scope: continuous systems such as continuous cellular automata, iterated maps and partial differential equations
measurable_quantities: occurrence of repetitive, nested, random and localized-structure behavior in continuous rule families
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Adding dimensions does not fundamentally change the occurrence of complexity
claims.claim: Contrary to what traditional science suggests, going from one to two or more dimensions produces some specific new effects but does not fundamentally change the overall behavior or the occurrence of complexity in simple programs.
claims.quote: adding more dimensions does not ultimately seem to have much effect on the occurrence of behavior of any significant complexity.
claims.scope: simple programs (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems) in one, two and three dimensions
measurable_quantities: fraction of rules showing complex behavior by dimension
classes of behavior by dimension
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating cellular automaton and Turing machine rules in several dimensions.

claims.label: Slices of 2D cellular automata resemble 1D cellular automata
claims.claim: The complexity inside patterns generated by two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata is very similar to that of one-dimensional cellular automata: a one-dimensional slice through the 2D pattern evolves much like an ordinary 1D cellular automaton.
claims.quote: if one looks at the evolution of a one-dimensional slice through each two-dimensional pattern the results one gets are strikingly similar to what we have seen in ordinary one-dimensional cellular automata.
claims.scope: two-dimensional outer totalistic cellular automata from a single seed
measurable_quantities: space-time patterns of central slices
comparison with 1D elementary cellular automaton classes
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with cellular automaton simulation software.

claims.label: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles
claims.claim: Some simple two-dimensional cellular automata on a square grid grow patterns whose overall shape closely approximates a perfect circle, despite the grid's square symmetry.
claims.quote: it is even possible to find cellular automata that yield overall shapes that closely approximate perfect circles.
claims.scope: two-dimensional outer totalistic cellular automata with 8 neighbors
measurable_quantities: deviation of pattern boundary from a circle
growth rate of radius with steps
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with cellular automaton simulation software.

claims.label: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors
claims.claim: A simple 2D cellular automaton (a cell turns black when exactly three of its eight neighbors are black, otherwise unchanged) can grow patterns whose overall shapes keep changing with no simple form, so complexity can appear in a pattern's overall shape as well as in its interior.
claims.quote: there can be great complexity not only in the detailed arrangement of black and white cells in a two-dimensional cellular automaton pattern, but also in the overall shape of the pattern.
claims.scope: two-dimensional growth-type cellular automata
measurable_quantities: boundary shape of growing patterns over time
whether growth stops
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with cellular automaton simulation software.

claims.label: Three-dimensional cellular automata show the same basic kinds of behavior
claims.claim: Three-dimensional cellular automata show some new specific phenomena but the same basic kinds of behavior as one- and two-dimensional ones, so the phenomenon of complexity does not depend crucially on dimensionality.
claims.quote: But overall it seems that the basic kinds of behavior produced are just the same as in one and two dimensions.
claims.scope: three-dimensional cellular automata
measurable_quantities: classes of behavior across sampled 3D rules
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable with cellular automaton simulation software.

claims.label: Complex behavior in 2D Turing machines is as rare as in 1D
claims.claim: Two-dimensional Turing machines behave much like one-dimensional ones: with two or three head states only repetitive and nested behavior normally occurs, and with four states complex behavior is possible but rare (a few rules per million).
claims.quote: For Turing machines with two or three possible states, only repetitive and nested behavior normally seem to occur. With four states, more complex behavior is possible, but it is still rather rare.
claims.scope: two-dimensional Turing machines with two to four head states and two colors
measurable_quantities: fraction of enumerated or randomly sampled rules showing non-nested behavior
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating or sampling two-dimensional Turing machine rules.

claims.label: Neighbor-independent geometric replacement rules always give nested fractals
claims.claim: Substitution systems and geometric replacement rules in which each element is replaced independently of other elements, including those of traditional fractal geometry, inevitably produce purely nested patterns.
claims.quote: with this kind of setup, it is ultimately inevitable that all the patterns produced must have a completely regular nested structure.
claims.scope: neighbor-independent two-dimensional substitution systems and iterated geometric replacement rules
claims.candidate_data: Standard results on self-similar sets and iterated function systems.

claims.label: Fractal geometry misses complexity by excluding interactions between elements
claims.claim: Traditional fractal geometry does not consider interactions between elements, which is why all patterns it produces are purely nested; allowing replacements to depend on neighbors on a grid readily yields complicated, non-nested patterns.
claims.quote: in traditional fractal geometry the idea of interaction between elements is not considered—so that all patterns that are produced have a purely nested form.
claims.scope: fractal geometry and two-dimensional neighbor-dependent substitution systems
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Networks of identical two-connection nodes can form arrays of any dimension
claims.claim: Networks in which every node is identical and has exactly two outgoing connections can, purely by the pattern of connections, form structures equivalent to arrays of any number of dimensions, as well as trees and nested structures.
claims.quote: using the same principles an array with any number of dimensions can easily be obtained.
claims.scope: directed networks with out-degree two
claims.candidate_data: Constructive proof by explicit network construction.

claims.label: Network rules depending on distance-two neighborhoods can give random growth
claims.claim: Network systems whose rewiring rules depend only on whether a node's two connections lead to the same node always grow in an essentially repetitive way, but when rules depend on nodes up to two connections away, even the number of nodes can vary in an apparently random way (in about one in 10,000 rules).
claims.quote: even the total number of nodes at each step can vary in a way that seems in many respects completely random.
claims.scope: network systems with local rewiring and node-insertion rules
measurable_quantities: node count per step
fraction of sampled rules with non-repetitive node counts
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by simulating network rewriting rules.

claims.label: Network systems may underlie the structure of space and spacetime
claims.claim: Some network systems will likely turn out to be closely related to the basic structure of space and spacetime in our universe.
claims.quote: I suspect that some of these systems will in the end turn out to be closely related to the basic structure of space and spacetime in our universe.
claims.scope: fundamental structure of physical space and spacetime
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Most multiway systems grow exponentially or not at all
claims.claim: Most multiway systems (which keep all sequences produced by all possible replacements at each step) either grow exponentially fast or do not grow at all; slow growth is rare.
claims.quote: most either grow exponentially quickly, or not at all; slow growth of the kind seen on the facing page is rather rare.
claims.scope: multiway (non-deterministic string rewriting) systems with simple rules
measurable_quantities: number of distinct states per step across enumerated rules
growth-rate classification
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating simple string rewriting rules.

claims.label: Slowly growing multiway systems eventually become repetitive
claims.claim: Even when slowly growing multiway systems show early apparent randomness in their state counts, they typically end up showing some form of repetition (sometimes with long periods, such as 1071 steps).
claims.quote: even when such growth leads to a certain amount of apparent randomness it typically in the end seems to exhibit some form of repetition.
claims.scope: slowly growing multiway systems
measurable_quantities: state counts per step
detected period of differences in state counts
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by simulating multiway systems.

claims.label: Multiway systems build their own network of connections in time
claims.claim: Because each sequence in a multiway system always leads to the same successors, the evolution can be represented as a network of which state leads to which, so multiway systems build up their own, often complicated, pattern of connections in time.
claims.quote: multiway systems can in effect build up their own pattern of connections in time—and this pattern can often be quite complicated.
claims.scope: multiway systems
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern
claims.claim: In one dimension, any set of local constraints on cell colors that can be satisfied at all can be satisfied by a simple, purely repetitive arrangement, so simple 1D constraints cannot force complex patterns.
claims.quote: in one dimension it is possible to prove that any local set of constraints that can be satisfied at all can always be satisfied by some simple and purely repetitive arrangement of colors.
claims.scope: one-dimensional local constraint systems (one-dimensional subshifts of finite type)
claims.candidate_data: Standard results in symbolic dynamics.

claims.label: All satisfiable 2D nearest-neighbor template constraints allow repetitive patterns
claims.claim: Of all 4,294,967,296 two-dimensional constraints defined by allowed templates of a cell and its four neighbors, 766,979,044 cannot be satisfied, and every one of the rest can be satisfied by a repetitive pattern, with 171 repetitive patterns sufficing for all.
claims.quote: among the 3,527,988,252 that remain, it turns out that every single one can be satisfied by a simple repetitive pattern.
claims.scope: two-dimensional two-color constraints on five-cell (von Neumann) neighborhood templates
measurable_quantities: count of unsatisfiable constraint sets
number of distinct repetitive patterns needed
claims.candidate_data: Reproducible by exhaustive computer search with tiling and SAT-solver tools.

claims.label: Constraint systems require going outside the system to find their patterns
claims.claim: Unlike rule-based systems, which can be run directly, systems defined by constraints offer no direct procedure for finding the patterns they allow; one must search from outside the system, which can take enormous computational effort.
claims.quote: But in a system that is based on constraints, there is no such direct procedure, and instead one must in effect always go outside of the system to work out what patterns can occur.
claims.scope: systems defined by constraints versus explicit evolution rules
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: The simplest constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern forces a nested one
claims.claim: Among 2D template constraints that also require one template to appear somewhere, systematic search over more than 18 million constraints finds that the first constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern (number 18762389) forces a unique nested pattern.
claims.quote: after examining more than 18 million of them, one finally discovers the system shown on the facing page. And in this system, unlike all others before it, no repetitive pattern is possible; the only pattern that satisfies the constraint is the non-repetitive nested pattern shown in the picture.
claims.scope: two-dimensional template constraints with a required-template condition
measurable_quantities: position in enumeration of first constraint forcing non-periodicity
structure of the forced pattern
claims.candidate_data: Reproducible by computer search; related literature on aperiodic tilings and Wang tiles.

claims.label: No tested simple template constraint forces more than nested behavior
claims.claim: Of the 137,438,953,472 template constraints with a required-template condition, none of the millions tested forces anything more complicated than nested behavior.
claims.quote: of the millions of these that I have tested, none have forced anything more complicated than the kind of nested behavior seen on the previous page.
claims.scope: two-dimensional template constraints with a required-template condition
measurable_quantities: fraction of tested constraints forcing non-repetitive, nested or more complex patterns
claims.candidate_data: Reproducible by computer search with SAT solvers.

claims.label: 3x3 template constraints can force a rule 30–like random pattern
claims.claim: Constraints on 3×3 blocks of cells can be constructed to force complex patterns: a set of 56 allowed templates forces a unique, largely random pattern equivalent to the evolution of the rule 30 cellular automaton.
claims.quote: a system with 56 allowed templates in which the only pattern satisfying the constraint is a complex and largely random one, derived from the rule 30 cellular automaton.
claims.scope: two-dimensional constraints on 3×3 neighborhoods
claims.candidate_data: Verifiable by explicit construction and SAT-based checking.

claims.label: Simple constraints rarely force complex behavior, unlike simple rules
claims.claim: Unlike simple evolution rules, almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns; complex behavior forced by constraints is rare.
claims.quote: it seems that almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns.
claims.scope: constraint-based systems compared with rule-based simple programs
measurable_quantities: fraction of constraint sets forcing non-repetitive patterns versus fraction of rules producing complex behavior
claims.candidate_data: Directly computable by enumerating constraint systems and cellular automaton rules.

claims.label: Constraint-like equations helped hide complexity from traditional science
claims.claim: Because describing complex behavior with constraints requires fairly complicated constraints, the traditional focus of science and mathematics on equations that act like constraints is another reason they failed to identify the phenomenon of complexity.
claims.quote: the fact that traditional science and mathematics tends to concentrate on equations that operate like constraints provides yet another reason for their failure to identify the fundamental phenomenon of complexity that I discuss in this book.
claims.scope: methods of traditional science and mathematics
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Simple systems self-organize from random initial conditions
