claims.claim: Many simple-rule systems such as cellular automata, when started from completely random initial conditions, spontaneously organize themselves and produce behavior with many distinctly non-random features.
claims.quote: many systems spontaneously tend to organize themselves, so that even with completely random initial conditions they end up producing behavior that has many features that are not at all random.
claims.scope: cellular automata and similar simple programs started from random initial conditions
measurable_quantities: entropy or block-frequency statistics of configurations over time
density of cells over time
frequency of emergent localized structures
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of elementary and totalistic cellular automata with public tools such as Wolfram Language CellularAutomaton or open-source CA libraries.

claims.label: Cellular automaton behavior falls into four basic classes
claims.claim: Despite differing in detail for almost every rule, the patterns produced by cellular automata of all kinds from random initial conditions can almost always be easily assigned to one of just four classes: uniform final state (class 1), simple stable or periodic structures (class 2), apparently random behavior (class 3), and interacting localized structures (class 4).
claims.quote: among all kinds of cellular automata, it seems that the patterns which arise can almost always be assigned quite easily to one of just four basic classes illustrated below.
claims.scope: all kinds of cellular automata evolved from random initial conditions
measurable_quantities: class assignment for each rule in an enumerated rule space
fraction of rules not cleanly classifiable
agreement between visual and quantitative classifications
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive simulation of elementary (256) and small totalistic cellular automaton rule spaces, plus published automated CA classification studies using compression or entropy measures.

claims.label: Class 4 consists of simple localized structures interacting in complex ways
claims.claim: Class 4 cellular automata mix order and randomness: they produce localized structures that are individually fairly simple, but which move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.
claims.quote: class 4 involves a mixture of order and randomness: localized structures are produced which on their own are fairly simple, but these structures move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.
claims.scope: class 4 cellular automata
measurable_quantities: number and types of localized structures (gliders)
collision outcomes between structures
claims.candidate_data: Simulation of known class 4 rules (rule 110, Game of Life, totalistic codes) and published glider catalogs for rule 110 and the Game of Life.

claims.label: Detailed cellular automaton properties correlate with the four classes
claims.claim: Most detailed properties of cellular automata correlate closely with the four visually defined classes, so that knowing a cellular automaton's class is often enough to predict its detailed properties.
claims.quote: most of these properties were closely correlated with the classes that I had already identified. Indeed, in trying to predict detailed properties of a particular cellular automaton, it was often enough just to know what class the cellular automaton was in.
claims.scope: cellular automata in general
measurable_quantities: Lyapunov-like damage-spreading rates
entropy and compressibility of patterns
repetition periods on finite lattices
correlation of these with class labels
claims.candidate_data: Simulation of enumerated cellular automaton rule spaces with computed statistics compared against class labels, plus published CA classification literature.

claims.label: A cellular automaton's class usually cannot be read off its rule
claims.claim: For most cellular automata there is no easy way to determine from the underlying rule which class of behavior it will produce; one generally has to run it and see, though some rule forms can be shown to give only class 1 or 2 behavior.
claims.quote: In most cases there is no easy way to do this, and in fact there is little choice but just to run the cellular automaton and see what it does.
claims.scope: predicting cellular automaton behavior class from rule specification
measurable_quantities: accuracy of rule-table features (e.g. Langton lambda) in predicting class
claims.candidate_data: Simulation of enumerated rule spaces and published studies of rule-table parameters as predictors of CA class.

claims.label: Class 4 lies between class 2 and class 3 in activity
claims.claim: Although class 4 is the most complex in appearance, in terms of overall activity it is intermediate between class 2 and class 3, and in sequences of rules it commonly appears at the transition between class 2 and class 3 rules.
claims.quote: Class 4 systems are then in the middle: for the activity that they show neither dies out completely, as in class 2, nor remains at the high level seen in class 3.
claims.scope: sequences of cellular automaton rules, both discrete and continuous
measurable_quantities: fraction of cells changing per step (activity) by class
location of class 4 rules within parameterized rule sequences
claims.candidate_data: Simulation of totalistic and continuous cellular automata across rule sequences, with measured activity per class.

claims.label: Continuous cellular automata show the same four classes
claims.claim: Cellular automata whose cells take continuous gray-level values show essentially the same four classes of behavior as discrete cellular automata, with class 4 behavior and its discrete localized structures typically appearing at transitions as the rule parameter is varied.
claims.quote: But it seems that this behavior falls into essentially the same four classes that we have already seen in ordinary cellular automata.
claims.scope: continuous cellular automata with a smoothly varying rule parameter
measurable_quantities: class of behavior as a function of the rule parameter
presence of localized structures near transitions
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of continuous cellular automata of the averaging-plus-constant type with standard numerical tools.

claims.label: Two-dimensional cellular automata show the same four classes
claims.claim: Two-dimensional cellular automata exhibit the same four classes of behavior as one-dimensional ones, which becomes evident when one-dimensional slices through their evolution are examined; class 4 behavior, as in the Game of Life, occurs even on a white background with slightly more complicated rules.
claims.quote: Indeed, by looking at such slices one can readily identify the very same four classes of behavior as in one-dimensional cellular automata.
claims.scope: two-dimensional cellular automata
measurable_quantities: class assignment of 2D rules from space-time slices
statistics of slices compared to 1D patterns
claims.candidate_data: Simulation of 2D totalistic rules and the Game of Life with tools such as Golly or Wolfram Language, plus the LifeWiki pattern collection.

claims.label: The four classes respond differently to small changes in initial conditions
claims.claim: Changing one cell of the initial condition has characteristically different effects by class: in class 1 the change dies out, in class 2 it stays localized, in class 3 it spreads at a uniform rate to affect the whole system, and in class 4 it spreads only sporadically.
claims.quote: In class 1, changes always die out, and in fact exactly the same final state is reached regardless of what initial conditions were used. In class 2, changes may persist, but they always remain localized in a small region of the system.
claims.scope: cellular automata of all four classes
measurable_quantities: Hamming distance between perturbed and unperturbed evolutions over time
spreading speed of the difference pattern
claims.candidate_data: Damage-spreading simulations of cellular automata with public tools, and published damage-spreading studies.

claims.label: Natural systems can be understood by how they handle information
claims.claim: Some of the most important features of natural systems can often be understood just by identifying which cellular automaton class their handling of information (forgetting, localized retention, long-range communication) corresponds to.
claims.quote: it is often possible to understand some of the most important features of systems that occur in nature just by looking at how their handling of information corresponds to what we have seen in the basic classes of systems that we have identified here.
claims.scope: natural systems in general
measurable_quantities: perturbation-propagation behavior in natural systems
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Systems of Limited Size and Class 2 Behavior
claims.label: Class 2 repetitiveness stems from lack of long-range communication
claims.claim: Class 2 cellular automata are always eventually repetitive because their lack of long-range communication makes each part behave as an independent system of limited size, typically only a few cells across, and hence with short repetition periods.
claims.quote: the absence of long-range communication effectively forces each part of a class 2 system to behave as if it were a system of limited size.
claims.scope: class 2 cellular automata
measurable_quantities: sizes of independent regions
repetition periods of regions in class 2 evolutions
claims.candidate_data: Simulation of class 2 elementary and totalistic cellular automata from random initial conditions.

claims.section: Systems of Limited Size and Class 2 Behavior
claims.label: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat
claims.claim: Any system of limited size made of discrete elements and following definite rules must eventually exhibit repetitive behavior, with repetition period at most equal to its total number of possible states.
claims.quote: it is then a general result that any system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules must always eventually exhibit repetitive behavior.
claims.scope: finite-state deterministic discrete systems
measurable_quantities: repetition period versus number of possible states
claims.candidate_data: Standard pigeonhole-principle proof; checkable by simulation of finite cellular automata.

claims.section: Systems of Limited Size and Class 2 Behavior
claims.label: Repetition periods of class 3 rules grow rapidly with system size
claims.claim: In cellular automata on a finite cyclic lattice, a rapid increase of repetition period with lattice size is characteristic of class 3 behavior, with large fluctuations as size changes; among elementary rules only rule 45 appears to give periods always near the maximum possible.
claims.quote: In general, a rapid increase with size is characteristic of class 3 behavior. Of the elementary rules, however, only rule 45 seems to yield periods that always stay close to the maximum of 2^n.
claims.scope: elementary cellular automata on cyclic lattices of size n
measurable_quantities: repetition period as a function of lattice size n for each rule
claims.candidate_data: Direct computation of cycle lengths for elementary cellular automata on small cyclic lattices, and OEIS entries for related cycle-length sequences.

claims.label: Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions
claims.claim: The randomness of class 3 systems is not merely inherited from random initial conditions: random behavior can be generated even when the initial conditions contain no randomness at all.
claims.quote: the crucial point that I discovered only some time later is that random behavior can also occur even when there is no randomness in initial conditions.
claims.scope: class 3 cellular automata such as rule 30 and rule 22
measurable_quantities: statistical randomness tests on patterns from simple initial conditions
similarity of statistics from simple versus random initial conditions
claims.candidate_data: Simulation of rule 30 and other rules with statistical test suites such as NIST SP 800-22 or Dieharder.

claims.label: Additive rule 90 only transmits randomness from its initial conditions
claims.claim: Because rule 90 is additive, its patterns are superpositions of the single-cell nested pattern, so it cannot generate randomness intrinsically; any randomness it shows comes from the initial conditions, and deviations such as a low initial density persist forever, unlike in rule 22.
claims.quote: In rule 22 the low initial density has no long-term effect. But in rule 90 its effect continues forever.
claims.scope: additive cellular automata (rule 90) versus non-additive class 3 rules (rule 22)
measurable_quantities: cell density over time from low-density random initial conditions
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rules 22 and 90; additivity of rule 90 is provable by linear algebra over GF(2).

claims.label: Intrinsic randomness generation makes large-scale behavior stable
claims.claim: Systems that intrinsically generate randomness, like rule 22 or rule 30, produce the same overall random behavior with the same large-scale properties whatever their initial conditions, giving them a fundamental stability that he says underlies the apparent stability of many systems in nature.
claims.quote: By intrinsically generating randomness such systems in a sense have a certain fundamental stability: for whatever is done to their initial conditions, they still give the same overall random behavior, with the same large-scale properties.
claims.scope: intrinsically random cellular automata and natural systems with apparent stability
measurable_quantities: large-scale statistics (density, block frequencies) as a function of initial-condition statistics
claims.candidate_data: Simulation of rule 22 and rule 30 from varied initial conditions; no specific natural-system dataset known.

claims.label: Spatially periodic initial conditions always give repetitive behavior
claims.claim: In any cellular automaton, an initial condition consisting of a fixed block of n cells repeated forever leads to repetitive behavior with period at most 2^n, since each block evolves like a finite cyclic system.
claims.quote: in any cellular automaton it is inevitable that initial conditions which consist just of a fixed block of cells repeated forever will lead to simple repetitive behavior.
claims.scope: all cellular automata with spatially periodic initial conditions
measurable_quantities: repetition period as a function of block width
claims.candidate_data: Elementary proof from the finite-state argument; verifiable by simulation.

claims.label: Special initial conditions often make one cellular automaton emulate another
claims.claim: It is common for a cellular automaton to have special initial conditions under which it behaves exactly like some other cellular automaton; for example rule 126 behaves like rule 90 when started from paired-cell blocks, and class 3 rules can thereby act like class 2 rules.
claims.quote: it turns out to be quite common for there to exist special initial conditions for one cellular automaton that make it behave just like some other cellular automaton.
claims.scope: cellular automata and their block emulations
measurable_quantities: existence of block encodings mapping one rule's evolution onto another's
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive search of block encodings among elementary cellular automata by computation.

claims.label: Nested patterns arise from rules that emulate themselves
claims.claim: A cellular automaton whose blocks of cells evolve by the same rule as individual cells must produce patterns that are either essentially uniform or nested; this self-emulation is why rule 90 and rules that emulate it produce nested patterns.
claims.quote: And this can be achieved in only two ways: either the pattern must be essentially uniform, or it must have a nested structure—just like we see in rule 90.
claims.scope: self-emulating cellular automata
measurable_quantities: self-similarity (fractal dimension) of patterns from self-emulating rules
claims.candidate_data: Computation of patterns and block-renormalization checks for elementary cellular automata.

claims.label: Additive rules self-emulate; rules 90 and 150 are the only elementary ones
claims.claim: Every additive cellular automaton rule can emulate itself and therefore yields nested patterns, and among two-color nearest-neighbor rules the only fundamentally different additive rules are rules 90 and 150; self-emulation is otherwise rare, though non-additive examples such as rule 184 exist.
claims.quote: one can show that any rule that is additive will be able to emulate itself and will thus yield nested patterns. But there are rather few additive rules, and indeed with two colors and nearest neighbors the only fundamentally different ones are precisely rules 90 and 150.
claims.scope: additive cellular automata, especially elementary rules
measurable_quantities: enumeration of additive elementary rules
block self-emulation check for each rule
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive enumeration over the 256 elementary rules and standard results on linear cellular automata over finite fields.

claims.label: Allowed-sequence networks grow fast for class 3 and 4, slowly for 1 and 2
claims.claim: As cellular automata evolve, the set of cell sequences that can occur generally becomes progressively restricted; the finite networks describing these sets stay simple (about t^2 nodes after t steps) for class 1 and 2 rules but grow at least exponentially for most class 3 and 4 rules, apart from surjective rules started from all possible sequences.
claims.quote: Indeed, this kind of rapid increase in network complexity is a general characteristic of most class 3 and 4 rules.
claims.scope: one-dimensional cellular automata and the regular languages of their configurations
measurable_quantities: number of nodes in minimal finite automata for allowed sequences after t steps
claims.candidate_data: Computation of regular-language images of cellular automaton maps with automata-theory tools, and published studies of CA regular-language complexity.

claims.label: Class 4 systems always have structures that persist forever
claims.claim: A crucial feature of any class 4 cellular automaton is that, although most structures that form eventually die out, there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.
claims.quote: Most of these structures eventually die out, sometimes in rather complicated ways. But a crucial feature of any class 4 systems is that there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.
claims.scope: class 4 cellular automata
measurable_quantities: catalog of persistent structures found by searching initial conditions
survival fraction of structures
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive initial-condition searches by simulation, and published glider catalogs for rule 110 and the Game of Life.

claims.label: Complicated persistent structures imply moving structures exist
claims.claim: In class 4 cellular automata, whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found; moving structures are what allow information to travel and complex class 4 behavior to occur.
claims.quote: My experience with many different rules is that whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found.
claims.scope: class 4 cellular automata
measurable_quantities: presence of stationary versus moving persistent structures in searched rules
claims.candidate_data: Glider searches over class 4 rules by simulation, and existing glider catalogs for the Game of Life and rule 110.

claims.label: Class 4 automata can mimic many other systems
claims.claim: Class 4 cellular automata can, with appropriate initial conditions, mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems, including producing unbounded growth of either complex or very simple form.
claims.quote: it is a general feature of class 4 cellular automata that with appropriate initial conditions they can mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems.
claims.scope: class 4 cellular automata
measurable_quantities: range of behaviors obtainable from special initial conditions
existence of emulations of other systems
claims.candidate_data: Simulation and construction of emulations in known class 4 rules such as rule 110 and the Game of Life.

claims.label: Interactions among simple structures in rule 110 give immense complexity
claims.claim: Although individual persistent structures in class 4 systems such as rule 110 behave fairly repetitively, collisions between them can produce cascades of new structures and outcomes that take very many steps to resolve, yielding behavior of immense complexity from an extremely simple rule.
claims.quote: So even though the individual structures in class 4 systems like rule 110 may behave in fairly repetitive ways, interactions between these structures can lead to behavior of immense complexity.
claims.scope: rule 110 and other class 4 cellular automata
measurable_quantities: collision outcomes and their resolution times for pairs of rule 110 structures
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 110 collisions and published rule 110 glider collision catalogs.

claims.label: Universal behavior types span simple programs and natural systems
claims.claim: The same kinds of overall behavior arise regardless of the details of underlying rules, and this universality holds not only among simple programs but also between simple programs and systems in nature, so idealized cell models and real molecular systems should show the same universal features.
claims.quote: And the crucial point is that I believe that this universality extends not only across simple programs, but also to systems in nature.
claims.scope: simple programs and natural systems with different underlying components
measurable_quantities: qualitative and statistical similarity of patterns produced by natural systems and by simple programs
claims.candidate_data: Published image collections of natural patterns (e.g. shells, crystals, fluid flows) compared against enumerations of simple programs computed in public software.

claims.label: Just three basic mechanisms account for randomness
claims.claim: Apparent randomness in any system arises from one of just three basic mechanisms: continual random input from the environment, randomness transcribed from initial conditions, or intrinsic generation of randomness by the system's own rules with no random input.
claims.quote: But from my investigations of simple programs I have come to the conclusion that one can in fact identify just three basic mechanisms for randomness, as illustrated in the pictures below.
claims.scope: all systems, natural or computational, that show apparent randomness
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Intrinsic randomness generation explains most randomness in nature
claims.claim: The mechanism in which a system's own deterministic rules generate randomness without any random input is ultimately responsible for a large fraction, and perhaps essentially all, of the randomness seen in the natural world.
claims.quote: I believe that this mechanism is in fact ultimately responsible for a large fraction, if not essentially all, of the randomness that we see in the natural world.
claims.scope: random-looking phenomena in the natural world
measurable_quantities: fraction of observed natural random phenomena attributable to intrinsic generation versus external noise or initial conditions
run-to-run repeatability of random details
claims.candidate_data: Replicate-run data from controlled physics, chemistry and fluid experiments, such as the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database for turbulent flows.

claims.label: Hardware noise-based random generators deviate from perfect randomness
claims.claim: Devices that generate randomness by amplifying microscopic environmental noise (spark gaps, vacuum tubes, semiconductor diodes) have consistently been found to produce output with significant deviations from perfect randomness, because the sampling device relaxes only gradually and because the environment itself has correlations.
claims.quote: But despite such sensitivity to microscopic effects, what has consistently been found in practice is that the output from such devices has significant deviations from perfect randomness.
claims.scope: physical random number generators based on electronic or other environmental noise
measurable_quantities: bias and serial correlation of raw hardware generator output
statistical test failure rates before post-processing
claims.candidate_data: Raw output from hardware random number generators analysed with standard test suites such as NIST SP 800-22, TestU01 or Dieharder.

claims.section: Chaos Theory and Randomness from Initial Conditions
claims.label: Randomness from initial conditions lasts only a limited number of steps
claims.claim: In physical chaotic systems such as kneading, mirror arrangements or pegboards, randomness can be attributed purely to initial conditions only for a small number of steps (around ten collisions for a pegboard), because amplification quickly reaches atomic scales and environmental perturbations take over; the limit is set by the separation between observed large-scale and uncontrollable small-scale features.
claims.quote: So the idea that randomness comes purely from initial conditions can be realistic only for a fairly small number of steps; randomness which is seen after that must therefore typically be attributed to other mechanisms.
claims.scope: physical systems with sensitive dependence on initial conditions
measurable_quantities: number of amplification steps or collisions before trajectories are dominated by environmental perturbations
ratio of observed to microscopic length scales
claims.candidate_data: Experimental trajectory data from Galton-board, billiard or chaotic-pendulum experiments with repeated runs.

claims.section: Chaos Theory and Randomness from Initial Conditions
claims.label: Solar system motion should show sensitive dependence over millions of years
claims.claim: Although planetary motion looks regular on human timescales, sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur in the solar system, producing significant randomness over a few million years that may explain some present-day features of the solar system.
claims.quote: But calculations imply that sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur even in our solar system.
claims.scope: orbital dynamics of planets and other bodies in the solar system
measurable_quantities: Lyapunov time of planetary orbits
divergence of numerical orbit integrations from nearby initial conditions
claims.candidate_data: JPL planetary ephemerides and published long-term numerical integrations of solar system orbits.

claims.label: Maximal-period linear congruential generators still show strong nonrandomness
claims.claim: Linear congruential random number generators designed to have maximal repetition period have repeatedly turned out to deviate substantially from perfect randomness (for example, successive outputs plotted as points fall on regular stripes), because the mathematical tractability that guarantees their period also implies regularity.
claims.quote: But in practice over the years, one after another linear congruential generator that has been constructed to have maximal repetition period has turned out to exhibit very substantial deviations from perfect randomness.
claims.scope: linear congruential pseudorandom number generators
measurable_quantities: lattice structure of successive output tuples (spectral test)
statistical test failure rates
claims.candidate_data: Direct computation of generators such as multiplier 65539 (RANDU) and evaluation with the spectral test or TestU01.

claims.label: Amenability to mathematical analysis implies deviations from randomness
claims.claim: The very possibility of detailed mathematical analysis of a system tends to imply that its output has at least some deviations from perfect randomness, whereas simple rules not constrained by the need for such analysis can generate highly random behavior.
claims.quote: the very possibility of any detailed mathematical analysis tends to imply the presence of at least some deviations from perfect randomness.
claims.scope: deterministic systems used to generate randomness, including pseudorandom generators
measurable_quantities: statistical quality of output from analytically tractable versus intractable generators
claims.candidate_data: Published comparisons of pseudorandom generators under TestU01 batteries.

claims.label: Rapid production of much randomness indicates intrinsic generation
claims.claim: Whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be responsible, because it uses every component of a system to produce new randomness and has no length limit, whereas environmental amplification is slow and initial-condition randomness is short-lived.
claims.quote: The basic answer, I believe, is that whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be the mechanism responsible.
claims.scope: natural and engineered systems that produce randomness
measurable_quantities: rate of randomness (entropy) production per unit time
dependence of output on environmental isolation
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Intrinsically generated randomness is repeatable across experimental runs
claims.claim: If randomness in an experiment comes from intrinsic generation, then even the precise details of the random-looking behavior should be repeatable from one run to the next, because such behavior is robust to perturbations below a critical size, whereas randomness from the environment or from initial conditions should show little or no repeatability.
claims.quote: But what is remarkable is that if intrinsic randomness generation is the mechanism at work, then the precise details of the behavior can also be repeatable.
claims.scope: carefully controlled experiments showing random-looking behavior
measurable_quantities: correlation of detailed random features between repeated runs of the same experiment
critical perturbation size below which behavior is unchanged
claims.candidate_data: Replicate-run datasets from controlled fluid, chemical or pattern-formation experiments, where published.

claims.label: Detailed visual similarities in organisms imply intrinsic randomness
claims.claim: Detailed visual similarities between members of the same species, and between the two symmetric sides of a system, in features that look complex and random cannot be attributed to environmental or initial-condition randomness and must come from intrinsic randomness generation.
claims.quote: And instead, there is no choice but to conclude that the randomness must in fact come from the mechanism of intrinsic randomness generation that I have discovered in simple programs, and discussed in this section.
claims.scope: complex-looking patterns in physical, biological and other systems, especially bilaterally symmetric ones
measurable_quantities: similarity of complex pattern details between left and right sides or between conspecific individuals
claims.candidate_data: Published image collections of animal pigmentation and shell patterns allowing left-right and between-individual comparisons.

claims.label: Randomness lets discrete components produce continuous behavior
claims.claim: Systems made of discrete components appear smooth and continuous on large scales mainly because microscopic randomness averages out the discreteness, and it does not matter whether that randomness comes from outside or from intrinsic generation, as shown by random walks, aggregation models and deterministic cellular automata that grow circular shapes.
claims.quote: But it turns out that all that really seems to matter is that randomness is present: the mechanism through which it arises appears to be largely irrelevant.
claims.scope: discrete systems such as random walks, aggregation models and cellular automata, and fluids made of molecules
measurable_quantities: isotropy and smoothness of large-scale shapes or distributions generated from discrete rules with external versus intrinsic randomness
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of random walks, Eden-type models and two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata in public software.

claims.label: Continuity requires slow features relative to small-scale random changes
claims.claim: Continuous large-scale behavior can arise in a system with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes; for growth, the random small-scale changes must occur much faster than the overall growth.
claims.quote: In general the point is that continuous behavior can arise in systems with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes.
claims.scope: discrete systems with randomness, including growth processes and domain coarsening
measurable_quantities: ratio of small-scale update rate to large-scale growth or boundary-motion rate
smoothness of resulting large-scale forms
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of cellular automata and growth models in public software.

claims.label: Density-driven discrete transitions are rare in 1D CAs, common in higher dimensions
claims.claim: Cellular automata in which a continuous change in initial density of black cells produces a discrete switch in long-time behavior, with whichever color was initially more common taking over the whole system, are fairly rare in one dimension, where domain boundaries often get stuck, but become increasingly common in two and more dimensions.
claims.quote: And so long as the boundaries of the regions do not get stuck—as happens in many one-dimensional cellular automata—the result is that whichever color was initially more common eventually takes over the whole system.
claims.scope: cellular automata in one, two and more dimensions started from random initial conditions of varying density
measurable_quantities: fraction of rules showing a discontinuous dependence of final density on initial density, by dimension
claims.candidate_data: Systematic enumeration and simulation of cellular automaton rule spaces in public software.

claims.label: Continuous rules can yield discrete behavior, so discrete models often fit
claims.claim: Even systems governed by continuous equations, such as certain chemical reaction kinetics, commonly have a limited number of stable states with discrete transitions between them, and because discrete overall behavior is often a system's most obvious feature, discrete models like cellular automata are often the most appropriate.
claims.quote: And in fact it is quite common for such behavior to be one of the most obvious features of a system—which is why discrete systems like cellular automata end up often being the most appropriate models.
claims.scope: natural systems with continuous underlying dynamics but discrete overall behavior, such as phase transitions and bistable chemical reactions
measurable_quantities: number of stable states and sharpness of transitions as parameters vary
claims.candidate_data: Experimental data on bistable chemical reactions and phase transitions in the published literature.

claims.label: Complex natural behavior is almost never best explained by constraints
claims.claim: Almost none of the complex behavior seen in nature is best explained as the satisfaction of constraints, because finding a pattern that satisfies a constraint is usually far too difficult a computation to happen routinely in nature; explicit processes of evolution are the more plausible explanation.
claims.quote: But despite this, my strong suspicion is that of all the examples of complex behavior that we see in nature almost none can in the end best be explained in terms of constraints.
claims.scope: complex behavior in physical and other natural systems
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Local-improvement procedures get stuck when satisfying discrete constraints
claims.claim: For discrete constraint systems the landscape of constraint violations is almost always jagged, so iterative procedures that only move downhill almost invariably get stuck far from a solution, random modifications help only slowly, and no speed-up techniques work well across broad classes of systems; hence natural systems are unlikely to come close to satisfying such constraints.
claims.quote: So what this suggests is that even if in some idealized sense a system in nature might be expected to satisfy certain constraints, it is likely that in practice the system will actually not have a way to come even close to doing this.
claims.scope: iterative and annealing-like procedures for discrete constraint satisfaction, and natural systems assumed to satisfy constraints
measurable_quantities: fraction of constraint violations remaining after a given number of local-update steps
time to reach exact solutions
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of local-search procedures on tiling and constraint problems, and published benchmarks for constraint-satisfaction and SAT solvers.

claims.label: Pushed or jiggled spheres do not reach densest packing
claims.claim: Unlike identical coins in two dimensions, which readily form the densest hexagonal packing when pushed together, balls in three dimensions pushed together or jiggled almost always get stuck and essentially never reach the densest repetitive packing, which seems obtainable only by careful one-by-one placement.
claims.quote: But if one just tries pushing balls together they almost always get stuck, and never take on anything like the arrangement shown.
claims.scope: packing of identical spheres and circles under physical compression or agitation
measurable_quantities: packing fraction achieved by compressed or vibrated sphere assemblies versus the face-centered cubic value
degree of crystalline order
claims.candidate_data: Published granular-packing experiments and simulations on random close packing of spheres.

claims.label: Complex biological forms come from growth rules, not selection-driven constraints
claims.claim: Natural selection can produce forms determined by constraint satisfaction only when those forms are rather simple; complex biological forms are associated instead with explicit evolution rules, mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.
claims.quote: when more complex forms are seen they once again tend to be associated not with constraints but rather with the effects of explicit evolution rules—mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.
claims.scope: biological forms shaped by natural selection and development
measurable_quantities: whether complex biological forms are reproduced by growth-rule models versus optimization/constraint models
claims.candidate_data: Published developmental-biology and morphogenesis datasets such as shell and leaf shape collections.

claims.label: Rule complexity does not determine behavioral complexity
claims.claim: There is no direct correspondence between the complexity of a system's underlying rules and the complexity of its behavior: some of the simplest rules yield highly complex behavior, fairly complicated rules often yield simple behavior, and rules differing at a single position can behave very differently.
claims.quote: Traditional intuition might have made one assume that there must be a direct correspondence between the complexity of observed behavior and the complexity of underlying rules. But one of the central discoveries of this book is that in fact there is not.
claims.scope: simple programs such as cellular automata, and by extension natural systems
measurable_quantities: correlation between rule description length and behavioral complexity measures across enumerated rules
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive enumeration of elementary and other cellular automata computed in public software.

claims.label: Nesting in nature mostly arises from building up, not splitting down
claims.claim: Nested patterns can arise either from elements splitting or branching into smaller ones or from larger elements being built up from smaller ones (as in additive cellular automata), and the building-up route is probably the more common origin of nesting in nature.
claims.quote: it can also arise when larger elements are built up from smaller ones—and indeed I suspect that this is its more common origin in nature.
claims.scope: nested (self-similar) patterns in natural systems
measurable_quantities: developmental or formation history of natural nested structures (splitting versus aggregation)
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Merging of independently growing domains generically produces nesting
claims.claim: Nesting can arise from random initial conditions through progressive annihilation of randomly placed elements: in essentially any system where domains grow fairly independently and then progressively merge, an overall nested pattern resembling a river-tributary tree forms, even when domain boundaries move as random walks.
claims.quote: And indeed in essentially any system where there are domains that grow fairly independently and then progressively merge the same basic overall nesting will be seen.
claims.scope: cellular automata such as rules 184 and 110 and other domain-coarsening systems from random initial conditions
measurable_quantities: scaling of domain sizes and branching statistics of annihilation trees over time
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 184, rule 110 and annihilating random walks in public software, plus river-network data such as HydroSHEDS for comparison.

claims.label: Models of complex systems should first be judged by comparing overall pictures
claims.claim: For systems with complex behavior, a model cannot be adequately assessed by matching a few extracted numbers; the best first test is a visual comparison of the model's overall behavior with that of the real system.
claims.quote: by far the best first step in assessing a model is not to look at numbers or other details, but rather just to use one's eyes, and to compare overall pictures of a system with pictures from the model.
claims.scope: scientific modelling of systems with complex behavior
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Snowflake shapes arise from growth inhibition captured by a hexagonal cellular automaton
claims.claim: The main features of snowflake shapes are reproduced by a hexagonal cellular automaton in which a cell becomes ice only if exactly one neighbor is ice, which represents the inhibition of nearby growth by released latent heat.
claims.quote: One can capture this basic effect by having a cellular automaton with rules in which cells become black if they have exactly one black neighbor, but stay white whenever they have more than one black neighbor.
claims.scope: growth of snowflakes (ice crystals from water vapor)
measurable_quantities: morphology of snowflakes compared with cellular automaton patterns at various steps
branching and faceting statistics of snow crystals
claims.candidate_data: Published snowflake photograph collections (e.g. W. A. Bentley's and K. Libbrecht's) and laboratory snow-crystal growth studies.

claims.label: Growing snowflakes should alternate between tree-like and faceted shapes
claims.claim: During the growth of an individual snowflake its shape should alternate between tree-like and faceted forms, as new branches grow and then collide with one another.
claims.quote: one expects that during the growth of a particular snowflake there should be alternation between tree-like and faceted shapes, as new branches grow but then collide with each other.
claims.scope: time course of individual snowflake growth
measurable_quantities: time-lapse sequence of snow crystal shape during growth
presence of facet-enclosed regions alternating with dendritic arms
claims.candidate_data: Laboratory time-lapse imaging of growing snow crystals and published snowflake photograph collections showing internal growth rings.

claims.label: Randomness in crystal shapes is often intrinsically generated by simple growth rules
claims.claim: Apparent randomness in the shapes of crystalline materials often arises intrinsically from simple deterministic growth rules, rather than from randomness in the seed or the growth environment.
claims.quote: And contrary to what has always been assumed, I suspect that this is actually how the apparent randomness that one sometimes sees in shapes formed by crystalline materials often comes about.
claims.scope: growth shapes of crystals
measurable_quantities: shape irregularity of crystals grown under controlled, uniform conditions from controlled seeds
reproducibility of crystal shapes across repeated growth runs
claims.candidate_data: Controlled crystal-growth experiments in the materials-science literature; no specific public dataset known.

claims.label: Randomness of fracture surfaces comes from a material-independent intrinsic mechanism
claims.claim: The roughness and randomness of fracture paths does not come from random irregularities in a material but from a general mechanism in which deterministic interactions of element displacements around a moving crack intrinsically generate randomness, as in a simple cellular automaton model.
claims.quote: I nevertheless suspect that even when much more realistic models for specific materials are used, the fundamental mechanisms responsible for randomness will still be very much the same as in the extremely simple model shown here.
claims.scope: fracture of solids, from single crystals to geological faults
measurable_quantities: roughness statistics of fracture surfaces in single crystals versus polycrystalline materials
scaling of fracture roughness across length scales
claims.candidate_data: Published fractography and fracture-surface roughness measurements (e.g. silicon single-crystal fracture studies and geological fault-surface profiles).

claims.label: Conservation plus microscopic randomness yields universal fluid behavior
claims.claim: Any system of particles that conserves quantities such as particle number and momentum and has sufficient microscopic randomness will show the same large-scale fluid behavior, so a discrete cellular automaton particle model can reproduce the flow of real fluids.
claims.quote: so long as certain physical quantities such as particle number and momentum are conserved, then whenever there is sufficient microscopic randomness, it is almost inevitable that the same overall fluid behavior will be obtained.
claims.scope: fluids and discrete lattice-gas models of fluids
measurable_quantities: large-scale velocity fields from lattice-gas simulations versus experiments at matched Reynolds number
eddy formation and shedding thresholds
claims.candidate_data: Lattice-gas and lattice-Boltzmann simulation codes and published experimental measurements of flow past cylinders (vortex shedding).

claims.label: Large-scale fluid flow shows little sensitive dependence on initial conditions
claims.claim: In almost all cases, large-scale fluid behavior does not depend discernibly on the detailed initial conditions; small perturbations are damped out by viscosity, so sensitive dependence (chaos) is the exception rather than the rule.
claims.quote: when it comes to large-scale fluid behavior, it seems to be true that in almost all cases there is no discernible difference between what happens with different detailed initial conditions.
claims.scope: large-scale behavior of real and model fluid flows, including turbulence
measurable_quantities: divergence of large-scale flow fields from slightly perturbed initial conditions
ensemble spread of repeated turbulence experiments
claims.candidate_data: Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database and direct numerical simulation codes, plus repeated-run laboratory flow experiments.

claims.label: Turbulent randomness is intrinsically generated at the level of large-scale fluid motion
claims.claim: The randomness seen in turbulent fluids is mostly neither inserted from outside nor inherited from molecular randomness, but is intrinsically generated by the dynamics of the large-scale fluid motion itself.
claims.quote: Instead, what seems to be happening is that intrinsic randomness generation occurs directly at the level of large-scale fluid motion.
claims.scope: turbulent fluid flow
measurable_quantities: randomness of large-scale flow under highly controlled, simple initial and boundary conditions
correlation between molecular-scale perturbations and large-scale flow
claims.candidate_data: Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database and published controlled turbulence experiments.

claims.label: Random-looking yet repeatable fluid flows should be producible
claims.claim: Because turbulent randomness is generated intrinsically by large-scale motion, carefully prepared experiments should produce fluid flows that look random yet are essentially the same on every repeated run.
claims.quote: with sufficiently careful preparation it should be possible to produce patterns of flow that seem quite random but that are nevertheless effectively repeatable—so that they look essentially the same on every successive run of an experiment.
claims.scope: laboratory fluid flows at turbulent or near-turbulent conditions
measurable_quantities: run-to-run correlation of complex flow patterns under identical preparation
complexity or entropy of the flow pattern
claims.candidate_data: Published vortex-interaction experiments; new repeated-run laboratory flow visualization would be needed.

claims.label: Evolution cannot have found optimal solutions to complex fitness constraints
claims.claim: Since iterative random search converges only for simple constraints, the roughly trillion generations of life on Earth are insufficient to find optimal solutions to complex constraints, so most features of organisms are merely good-enough solutions rather than optima.
claims.quote: it is still completely implausible that the trillion or so generations of organisms since the beginning of life on Earth would be sufficient to allow optimal solutions to be found to constraints of any significant complexity.
claims.scope: biological evolution as an iterative random search
measurable_quantities: convergence time of mutation-selection search on fitness landscapes of varying complexity
distance of observed traits from engineering optima
claims.candidate_data: Computational evolution and fitness-landscape simulations; published experimental evolution studies.

claims.label: Most biological complexity comes from randomly chosen programs, not natural selection
claims.claim: Most of the complexity seen in biological organisms originates from the abstract fact that many randomly chosen programs produce complex behavior, rather than from adaptation or careful optimization by natural selection.
claims.quote: the vast majority of the complexity we see in biological systems actually has its origin in the purely abstract fact that among randomly chosen programs many give rise to complex behavior.
claims.scope: complex forms and patterns in biological organisms
measurable_quantities: fitness effects of complex versus simple pattern details
frequency of complex behavior among random genetic or developmental variants
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Complexity of individual organism parts has been roughly constant for eons
claims.claim: The complexity of individual parts of organisms, such as textures and other morphological features, was already present in early fossils and has not changed much in at least several hundred million years.
claims.quote: there is every indication that the level of complexity of individual parts of organisms has not changed much in at least several hundred million years.
claims.scope: fossil record of morphological complexity
measurable_quantities: quantitative complexity measures of fossil textures and ornamentation over geological time
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database and published morphological-complexity time series from the fossil record.

claims.label: Genetic programs for complex pigment patterns are short
claims.claim: The genetic programs that generate patterns such as those on mollusc shells are short, as indicated by the large variety of patterns within species, and molecular biology should be able to isolate them and confirm their brevity.
claims.quote: Modern molecular biology should soon be able to isolate the specific programs responsible, say, for the patterns on mollusc shells, and see explicitly how long they are. But there are already indications that these programs are quite short.
claims.scope: genetic control of pigmentation patterns, especially on mollusc shells
measurable_quantities: number of genes and regulatory elements controlling shell pigmentation
intraspecific pattern variability
claims.candidate_data: Mollusc genome assemblies and shell-pigmentation gene-expression studies in NCBI GenBank and the published literature.

claims.label: Natural selection works meaningfully only on simple behavior
claims.claim: The power of natural selection is limited: it can systematically optimize only systems or parts of systems whose behavior is simple, and achieves very little when behavior is complex.
claims.quote: what I suspect is that in the end natural selection can only operate in a meaningful way on systems or parts of systems whose behavior is in some sense quite simple.
claims.scope: natural selection acting on biological traits
measurable_quantities: response to selection of simple versus complex traits
success of iterative random search on simple versus complex target behaviors
claims.candidate_data: Artificial-selection and experimental-evolution datasets; evolutionary computation benchmarks.

claims.label: Natural selection makes organisms simpler and more engineering-like
claims.claim: Rather than generating complexity, the main effect of natural selection is to make biological systems avoid complexity, favoring simple, somewhat independent components with smoothly adjustable properties, as in engineered systems.
claims.quote: my strong suspicion is that in fact the main effect of natural selection is almost exactly the opposite: it tends to make biological systems avoid complexity, and be more like systems in engineering.
claims.scope: biological organisms under natural selection
measurable_quantities: modularity and smoothness of variation in selected traits
complexity of traits under strong versus weak selection
claims.candidate_data: Quantitative-genetics datasets from plant and animal breeding; comparative morphology databases.

claims.label: Features that change fastest between species are the most complex
claims.claim: Among related species, the features that differ most rapidly (such as pigmentation and texture patterns) are the ones that show the most obvious complexity, while features under natural selection stay nearly constant.
claims.quote: it is almost always those features which change most rapidly between species that show the most obvious signs of complexity.
claims.scope: variation of traits among closely related species
measurable_quantities: rate of interspecific change of traits
complexity measure of each trait
claims.candidate_data: Comparative phylogenetic trait datasets and image collections of pigmentation in fishes, butterflies and molluscs.

claims.label: Convergent structures recur because they are common among programs, not optimal
claims.claim: When similar complex structures arise independently in very different organisms, this is because those structures are common outputs of programs of certain kinds, not because they are optimal.
claims.quote: the reason certain structures appear repeatedly is just that they are somehow common among programs of certain kinds
claims.scope: convergent evolution
measurable_quantities: frequency of convergent structures among outputs of random developmental programs
optimality of convergent structures
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Natural selection does not inherently drive organisms toward more elaborate structure
claims.claim: Natural selection does not inevitably produce progressively more elaborate organisms; increases in complexity in the fossil record come from random mutations that add features without fatal flaws, while selection's systematic effect is to simplify.
claims.quote: It is certainly not the case—as is often assumed—that natural selection somehow inevitably leads to organisms with progressively more elaborate structures and progressively larger numbers of parts.
claims.scope: long-term trends in organismal complexity
measurable_quantities: trends in number of parts or cell types across lineages over time
frequency of simplification versus elaboration events
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database and published studies of trends in organismal complexity (e.g. cell-type counts across lineages).

claims.label: Plant branching patterns come from simple substitution-system growth rules
claims.claim: The overall branching patterns of plants, from algae to ferns to trees and flowering plants, are produced by simple growth rules in which each stem tip repeatedly splits into smaller copies of itself at fixed relative lengths and angles.
claims.quote: And no doubt it is from such simple rules of growth that most such overall branching patterns come.
claims.scope: overall branching architecture of plants
measurable_quantities: branch length ratios and branching angles
fit of substitution-system models to measured plant architectures
claims.candidate_data: Plant architecture measurements and L-system modelling literature; 3D plant scan datasets.

claims.label: Leaf shapes arise from the same simple branching process as whole plants
claims.claim: The shapes of leaves, from smooth to prickly to irregular, are produced by the same simple branching growth process that governs overall plant forms, and small changes in its parameters can change leaf shape greatly.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that in fact the very same simple process of branching is ultimately responsible both for the overall forms of plants, and for the shapes of their leaves.
claims.scope: leaf shape development in plants
measurable_quantities: leaf outline shapes versus outlines of substitution-system patterns
relation of early vein patterns to final leaf outlines
claims.candidate_data: Leaf image collections and herbarium digitizations (e.g. iDigBio, Leafsnap dataset) and leaf developmental studies.

claims.label: The 137.5° phyllotaxis angle results from a simple inhibition growth process
claims.claim: The near-universal 137.5° (golden-ratio) angle between successive plant organs is not an optimization found by natural selection but the inevitable result of a simple process where each new element forms where a chemical concentration is highest and depletes it nearby.
claims.quote: And instead what I strongly suspect is that the patterns are just inevitable consequences of a rather simple process of growth not unlike one that was already discussed, at least in general terms, nearly a century ago.
claims.scope: phyllotaxis and spiral arrangements of plant organs
measurable_quantities: divergence angles between successive organs
convergence of inhibition-model simulations to 137.5° across damping values
hormone concentration patterns at the shoot apex
claims.candidate_data: Published phyllotaxis divergence-angle measurements and auxin-distribution imaging studies of shoot apical meristems.

claims.label: Simple growth-rate models generate essentially all mollusc shell shapes
claims.claim: Mollusc shell shapes result from secreting material at different rates around the shell opening, and essentially every form produced by a simple growth model with a few parameters is found in some real mollusc.
claims.quote: The remarkable fact illustrated on the next page is that essentially all of them are found in some kind of mollusc or another.
claims.scope: coiled shell shapes of molluscs
measurable_quantities: shell growth parameters (expansion rate, translation, aperture shape) of real species
occupancy of the model parameter space by real species
claims.candidate_data: Shell morphometric datasets and museum shell collections; published theoretical-morphospace studies of coiled shells.

claims.label: Animal embryos develop hierarchically because of a fixed length scale
claims.claim: Because regions of tissue a few tenths of a millimeter across subdivide into regions using different sections of the genetic program (controlled by chemical gradients and homeobox genes), embryos necessarily develop hierarchically, e.g. a leg region before a foot region.
claims.quote: The existence of a fixed length scale at which such processes occur then almost inevitably implies that an embryo must develop in a somewhat hierarchical fashion.
claims.scope: embryonic development of animals
measurable_quantities: size of tissue regions at the time of subdivision
morphogen gradient length scales
order of appearance of nested anatomical regions
claims.candidate_data: Developmental biology atlases and morphogen-gradient measurements in the literature (e.g. Drosophila and vertebrate limb studies).

claims.label: Shape differences between related animals come from differing growth rates
claims.claim: Differences in shape among related animals are largely due to different patterns of relative growth rates of their parts, so their shapes are related by simple smooth geometric transformations.
claims.quote: differences between the shapes and forms of animals may often be due in large part merely to different patterns in the rates of growth for their different parts.
claims.scope: body shapes of animals within a family or order
measurable_quantities: geometric-morphometric landmark transformations between species
allometric growth coefficients
claims.candidate_data: Geometric morphometrics landmark datasets (e.g. MorphoSource specimen scans) and published allometry studies.

claims.label: Diversity of plant and animal forms comes from different simple rules
claims.claim: Most of the diversity and complexity in the forms of plants and animals arises because slightly different, essentially randomly picked simple growth rules lead to very different and often complex behavior.
claims.quote: it is this basic phenomenon that I suspect is responsible for most of the diversity and complexity that we see in the forms of plants and animals.
claims.scope: forms of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: sensitivity of developmental outcomes to small rule changes
match between simple-rule model outputs and observed morphological diversity
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Mollusc shell pigment patterns are generated like one-dimensional cellular automata
claims.claim: Pigmentation patterns on mollusc shells are produced line by line by pigment-secreting elements whose new states depend on neighbors' previous states, so the range of shell patterns closely matches the patterns of the simplest symmetric one-dimensional cellular automata.
claims.quote: comparing the patterns in these pictures with patterns on actual mollusc shells, one notices the remarkable fact that the range of patterns that occur in the two cases is extremely similar.
claims.scope: pigmentation patterns on mollusc shells
measurable_quantities: classification of shell patterns into cellular automaton behavior classes
statistical comparison of shell pattern features with cellular automaton outputs
claims.candidate_data: Published shell-pattern image collections and museum mollusc collections.

claims.label: Mollusc shell pattern rules are effectively random, not optimized
claims.claim: The rules generating mollusc shell patterns are effectively chosen at random from the simplest possibilities rather than optimized against predators or for mates, as shown by many species whose patterns are hidden by opaque skin throughout life.
claims.quote: these patterns are instead generated by rules that are in effect chosen at random from among a collection of the simplest possibilities.
claims.scope: evolution of mollusc shell pigmentation
measurable_quantities: prevalence of complex patterns in species whose shells are covered in life
phylogenetic signal and selective correlates of shell patterns
claims.candidate_data: Museum mollusc collections with periostracum and habitat records; comparative phylogenetic studies of shell coloration.

claims.label: Animal coat patterns arise from local activation and longer-range inhibition rules
claims.claim: The few recurring kinds of animal pigmentation patterns (spots, labyrinths, stripes) are produced by a simple rule in which each element tends to match the average color of nearby elements and oppose that of elements further away, as in a two-dimensional cellular automaton.
claims.quote: The idea is that when a pattern forms, the color of each element will tend to be the same as the average color of nearby elements, and opposite to the average color of elements further away.
claims.scope: pigmentation patterns on animal skins and coats
measurable_quantities: spatial statistics of real coat patterns versus model outputs
short-range activation and long-range inhibition between pigment cells
claims.candidate_data: Animal coat-pattern image collections and published zebrafish pigment-cell interaction experiments.

claims.label: Short-timescale market randomness comes from internal market dynamics
claims.claim: Much of the apparent randomness in financial prices, especially on timescales of minutes or seconds, is generated by the internal dynamics of trading entities interacting with one another, not by external news or changes in the value of the asset.
claims.quote: particularly on short timescales much of the randomness that one sees is purely a consequence of internal dynamics in the market, and has little if anything to do with the nature or value of what is being traded.
claims.scope: price fluctuations in financial markets
measurable_quantities: intraday price volatility versus news arrival
volatility during purely speculative trading
autocorrelation and entropy of high-frequency returns
claims.candidate_data: CRSP or other market tick data (e.g. NYSE TAQ) combined with timestamped news feeds.

claims.label: Simple cellular automaton markets generate random-looking price series
claims.claim: In a market modelled as a one-dimensional cellular automaton of buy/sell agents reacting to neighbors, any rule that lets information eventually propagate to all agents makes the running buy-minus-sell total show significant randomness.
claims.quote: as soon as the underlying rule for the cellular automaton is such that information will eventually propagate from one entity to all others—in effect a minimal version of an efficient market hypothesis—it is essentially inevitable that running totals of numbers of cells will exhibit significant randomness.
claims.scope: one-dimensional cellular automaton models of markets
measurable_quantities: randomness tests on running totals of cell colors for all rules with full information propagation
claims.candidate_data: Direct enumeration and simulation of elementary cellular automata with standard software.

claims.label: A very simple program may underlie all of physics
claims.claim: Underneath the known laws of physics there may be a single very simple program from which all known laws, and all the complexity of the universe, emerge.
claims.quote: Underneath the laws of physics as we know them today it could be that there lies a very simple program from which all the known laws—and ultimately all the complexity we see in the universe—emerges.
claims.scope: the fundamental laws of the universe
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Reversible rules are rare among cellular automata
claims.claim: Reversibility is rare among simple cellular automaton rules: only 6 of the 256 elementary two-color nearest-neighbor rules are reversible, and only 1800 of the 7,625,597,484,987 three-color nearest-neighbor rules are.
claims.quote: There are a total of 7,625,597,484,987 cellular automata with three colors and nearest-neighbor rules, and searching through these one finds just 1800 that are reversible.
claims.scope: one-dimensional cellular automata with two and three colors and nearest-neighbor rules
measurable_quantities: number of reversible (injective) rules among elementary and three-color nearest-neighbor cellular automata
claims.candidate_data: Computational enumeration using standard reversibility tests for one-dimensional cellular automata (e.g. de Bruijn graph or Amoroso–Patt style algorithms) in public software.

claims.section: Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
claims.label: Reversible systems can behave as complexly as any other
claims.claim: Although only a tiny fraction of possible rules are reversible, reversible cellular automata can still produce behavior, including apparent randomness and localized structures, as complex as that of non-reversible systems.
claims.quote: So in the end it seems that even though only a very small fraction of possible systems have the property of being reversible, such systems can still exhibit behavior just as complex as one sees anywhere else.
claims.scope: reversible cellular automata, including second-order rules constructed to be time-reversal symmetric
measurable_quantities: complexity or randomness measures (e.g. entropy, compressibility) of patterns from reversible versus non-reversible rules
presence of localized structures
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of reversible second-order and three-color cellular automata with open-source tools.

claims.section: Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
claims.label: Second Law holds because experiments cannot prepare randomness-decreasing states
claims.claim: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is observed to hold because practical experiments can only set up initial conditions that are simple to describe and construct, and finding initial conditions of a reversible system that would lead to decreasing randomness requires computation as great as the system's own evolution.
claims.quote: The consequence of this is that no reasonable experiment can ever involve setting up the kind of initial conditions that will lead to decreases in randomness, and that therefore all practical experiments will tend to show only increases in randomness.
claims.scope: reversible physical systems and the experiments performed on them; origin of the Second Law of Thermodynamics
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
claims.label: Reversible rule 37R does not obey the Second Law
claims.claim: The reversible cellular automaton rule 37R, even as a closed system, shows neither a systematic trend toward increasing randomness nor simple predictable behavior, but fluctuates indefinitely between more and less ordered states, so it does not obey the Second Law for practical purposes.
claims.quote: There is, I believe, no choice but to conclude that for practical purposes rule 37R simply does not obey the Second Law.
claims.scope: the second-order reversible elementary cellular automaton rule 37R in finite closed regions
measurable_quantities: coarse-grained entropy over time
recurrence period
fraction of state space visited from given initial conditions
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 37R with open-source cellular automaton code, computing coarse-grained entropy time series.

claims.section: Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
claims.label: Biological order arises from partitioning into separated compartments
claims.claim: Biological systems can show increasing order despite the Second Law mainly because they partition into parts (cells, organisms) separated by membrane-like boundaries, within which organized behavior can occur while the boundary survives.
claims.quote: This basic mechanism may well be the main one at work in many biological systems: each cell or each organism becomes separated from others, and while it survives, it can exhibit organized behavior.
claims.scope: biological systems exhibiting self-organization
measurable_quantities: entropy production and order within compartmentalized versus non-compartmentalized systems
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
claims.label: The Second Law is general but not universally valid
claims.claim: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is an important and general principle but is not universally valid; many systems in nature behave like rule 37R and do not show a uniform trend toward increasing randomness.
claims.quote: And indeed I strongly suspect that there are many systems in nature which behave in more or less the same way. The Second Law is an important and quite general principle—but it is not universally valid.
claims.scope: physical, biological and other natural systems to which the Second Law is applied
measurable_quantities: entropy or disorder measures over time in closed natural systems outside gases
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Continuum behavior emerges from discrete randomizing conserving rules
claims.claim: Smooth continuum behavior, such as diffusion of density, emerges from discrete systems whenever small-scale apparent randomness washes out individual details and conserved quantities constrain overall features, as shown by block cellular automata whose average density follows the diffusion equation.
claims.quote: And much as in physical systems like fluids, what ultimately leads to this is the presence of small-scale apparent randomness that washes out details of individual cells or molecules—as well as of conserved quantities that force certain overall features not to change too quickly.
claims.scope: discrete systems with conserved quantities and intrinsic randomness, such as particle-conserving block cellular automata and fluids
measurable_quantities: ensemble-averaged density profiles over time compared with solutions of the diffusion equation
claims.candidate_data: Simulation of particle-conserving block cellular automata and lattice-gas models with open-source code.

claims.label: The fundamental rule cannot be found by working backwards from known laws
claims.claim: If the ultimate rule for the universe is simple, it cannot realistically be found by engineering it from observed features; the only practical method is to choose a straightforward representation and systematically search through large numbers of candidate rules.
claims.quote: my guess is that the only realistic way to find the rule in the first place will be to start from some very straightforward representation, and then just to search through large numbers of possible rules in this representation.
claims.scope: methodology for finding a fundamental theory of physics
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Space, gravity and quantum features are generic across many candidate rules
claims.claim: Features such as seemingly continuous space and certain aspects of gravitation and quantum mechanics will emerge from many different underlying rules for the universe, whereas properties like the spectrum of particle masses, and perhaps the dimensionality of space, will be specific to particular rules.
claims.quote: so also I suspect that properties such as the existence of seemingly continuous space, as well as certain features of gravitation and quantum mechanics, will emerge with many different possible underlying rules for the universe.
claims.scope: candidate fundamental rules for the universe
measurable_quantities: fraction of candidate network rules whose large-scale behavior shows finite-dimensional space or Einstein-like behavior
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Most known physical laws are emergent, not fundamental
claims.claim: Most physical laws discovered so far are not fundamental but are emergent large-scale features of an underlying rule, so their simplicity says little about the simplicity of that rule.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that the vast majority of physical laws discovered so far are not truly fundamental, but are instead merely emergent features of the large-scale behavior of some ultimate underlying rule.
claims.scope: known laws of physics
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Space is discrete below the scales probed by experiment
claims.claim: Space, though experimentally continuous down to about 10^-20 meters, is very likely made of discrete elements at still smaller scales, just as fluids and other seemingly continuous things have turned out to be.
claims.quote: Particle physics experiments have shown that space acts as a continuum down to distances of around 10^(-20) meters—or a hundred thousandth the radius of a proton. But there is absolutely no reason to think that discrete elements will not be found at still smaller distances.
claims.scope: the structure of physical space at very small distances
measurable_quantities: energy-dependent photon dispersion or Lorentz-violation bounds
deviations from continuum behavior at short distances
claims.candidate_data: Published Lorentz-invariance-violation bounds from gamma-ray burst timing (e.g. Fermi-LAT data) and high-energy collider results constrain but do not reach the scales proposed.

claims.label: Space and matter should be made of the same stuff
claims.claim: In the simplest ultimate model of the universe there is no distinction between space and its contents: matter and everything else are made of the same underlying structure as space, unlike in a cellular automaton.
claims.quote: But if the ultimate model for the universe is to be as simple as possible, then it seems much more plausible that both space and its contents should somehow be made of the same stuff—so that in a sense space becomes the only thing in the universe.
claims.scope: fundamental structure of space and matter
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: At the lowest level space is a network of nodes
claims.claim: At the lowest level, space is most likely a giant network of nodes defined only by their connections (and it suffices to consider nodes with exactly three connections), with ordinary space emerging as a large-scale limit.
claims.quote: And with this in mind I believe that what is by far the most likely is that at the lowest level space is in effect a giant network of nodes.
claims.scope: fundamental structure of physical space
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Network dimension is set by growth of node counts with distance
claims.claim: A network corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space exactly when the number of nodes within graph distance r of a node grows in a limiting sense like r^d; tree-like or randomly connected networks correspond to no finite dimension.
