claims.quote: in general the condition for a network to correspond to ordinary d-dimensional space is precisely that the total number of nodes that appear in it out to distance r grows in some limiting sense like r^d
claims.scope: large networks and their correspondence to finite-dimensional space
measurable_quantities: ball-volume growth exponent of graphs as a function of graph distance
claims.candidate_data: Computation on standard lattice, tree and random graphs with graph libraries such as NetworkX or igraph.

claims.label: Observers perceive time only through the causal network of events
claims.claim: An observer embedded in a system such as a mobile automaton cannot see its individual update steps; all the observer can perceive is the network of causal relationships between updating events, so perceived time and spacetime derive purely from that causal network, and sequential updating can appear as synchronized parallel evolution.
claims.quote: The most they will be able to tell is that a certain network of causal relationships exists—and their perception of time must therefore derive purely from the properties of this network.
claims.scope: observers embedded in discrete evolving systems, including the universe
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: The Sequencing of Events in the Universe
claims.label: Non-overlapping replacement rules give update-order-independent causal networks
claims.claim: A substitution system whose rules replace only blocks that can never overlap themselves or each other always yields the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are applied (the property Wolfram calls causal invariance).
claims.quote: And any substitution system whose rules specify replacements only for blocks such as these is guaranteed to yield the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are performed.
claims.scope: string substitution systems and, analogously, network rewriting systems
measurable_quantities: causal networks generated under different updating orders
claims.candidate_data: Computational checks with string-rewriting software and term-rewriting confluence results from the rewriting-systems literature.

claims.label: The universe's rules likely yield a unique causal network
claims.claim: Although the universe has no global clock and its rules may be applicable in arbitrary order, its actual rules most likely have the property of always yielding the same causal network, and so a unique perceived history.
claims.quote: it still tends to be my suspicion that there is not—and that in fact the particular rules followed by the universe do in the end have the property that they always yield the same causal network.
claims.scope: the fundamental update rules of the universe
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Small-scale randomness in the network makes space robustly 3D
claims.claim: The ultimate rules for the universe will produce networks that look largely random at small scales, and this randomness is what allows a definite and robust dimensionality of 3 to emerge for space.
claims.quote: my expectation is that they will give rise to networks that on a small scale look largely random. But this very randomness will most likely be what for example allows a definite and robust value of 3 to emerge for the dimensionality of space
claims.scope: network models of space and the dimensionality of physical space
measurable_quantities: effective dimension of networks generated by candidate rewriting rules
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Elementary length and time are tiny and their ratio is light speed
claims.claim: Each connection in the causal network of the universe corresponds to an identical elementary distance (perhaps about 10^-35 meters) and elementary time (perhaps about 10^-43 seconds), whose ratio is a fixed speed identified with the speed of light.
claims.quote: One may guess that this elementary distance is around 10^(-35) meters, and that the elementary time interval is around 10^(-43) seconds. But whatever these values are, a crucial point is that their ratio must be a fixed speed, and we can identify this with the speed of light.
claims.scope: discrete structure of spacetime
measurable_quantities: elementary length and time scales of spacetime
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Causal invariance yields special relativity
claims.claim: If the underlying rules of the universe are causal invariant, then slices through the causal network at different angles, corresponding to different uniform velocities, are all governed by the same rules, so physics is the same regardless of uniform motion and the standard phenomena of special relativity such as time dilation follow.
claims.quote: And the crucial point is that whenever the underlying system is causal invariant the exact same underlying rules will account for what one sees in slices at different angles. And what this means is that in effect the same rules will apply regardless of how fast one is going.
claims.scope: discrete causal network models of spacetime and special relativity
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Elementary particles are persistent localized structures in the network
claims.claim: Elementary particles are analogs of the localized structures seen in class 4 cellular automata: persistent structures (such as tangles or non-planar cores) in the network of space, so that the fundamental rules need make no reference to particular particles.
claims.quote: An immediate possibility that I suspect is actually not too far from the mark is that such particles are analogs of the localized structures that we saw earlier in this book in systems like the class 4 cellular automata shown below.
claims.scope: elementary particles of physics
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Fundamental particle masses may still have simple ratios
claims.claim: Although observed elementary particle masses are not in simple ratios (unlike electric charges), truly fundamental particle masses may still have simple relations, because observed masses include varying amounts of interaction energy.
claims.quote: But despite such results, it is still conceivable that there could in the end be simple relations between truly fundamental particle masses—since it turns out that the masses that have actually been observed in effect also include varying amounts of interaction energy.
claims.scope: masses of elementary particles such as leptons and quarks
measurable_quantities: measured particle masses and their ratios
estimates of interaction-energy contributions to masses
claims.candidate_data: Particle Data Group Review of Particle Physics mass tables.

claims.label: Network curvature appears in node counts via the Ricci scalar
claims.claim: In a large network approximating d-dimensional space, the leading correction to the number of nodes reached within distance r is proportional to the Ricci scalar curvature times r^(d+1), so curvature can be determined purely from network connectivity.
claims.quote: But in fact the leading correction to the number of nodes reached is always quite simple: it is just proportional to what is called the Ricci scalar curvature, multiplied by r^(d + 1).
claims.scope: large networks approximating curved Riemannian spaces
measurable_quantities: ball-volume growth corrections in graphs approximating curved manifolds
Ricci scalar curvature of the approximated manifold
claims.candidate_data: Known volume-of-geodesic-ball expansions in Riemannian geometry and numerical computation on graph discretizations of curved surfaces.

claims.label: Causal invariant dimension-preserving network rules give Einstein equations
claims.claim: Network replacement rules that are causal invariant and maintain a fixed number of dimensions will almost inevitably produce large-scale behavior close to the vacuum Einstein equations of general relativity, analogous to how Navier–Stokes behavior emerges from cellular automaton fluids.
claims.quote: But I suspect that if one has replacement rules that are causal invariant and that in effect successfully maintain a fixed number of dimensions they will almost inevitably lead to behavior that follows something close to the Einstein equations.
claims.scope: causal invariant network rewriting systems and general relativity
measurable_quantities: spacetime Ricci curvature estimated from event counts in causal-network cones
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Network-based programs will reproduce the key features of quantum theory
claims.claim: Discrete network models of the universe with causal invariance will ultimately turn out to exhibit many if not all of the key features of quantum theory, even though they are not set up in terms of its standard formalism.
claims.quote: And in fact it is my strong suspicion that the kinds of programs that I have discussed in the past few sections will actually in the end turn out to show many if not all the key features of quantum theory.
claims.scope: network models of the universe and quantum phenomena
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Network threads let deterministic models produce quantum correlations
claims.claim: The quantum correlations between distant particles usually taken to rule out definite underlying processes can arise in a deterministic network model, because particles created together stay linked by threads of connections that bypass ordinary three-dimensional space.
claims.quote: And the basic reason for this is that if the universe is a network then it can in a sense easily contain threads that continue to connect particles even when the particles get far apart in terms of ordinary space.
claims.scope: correlations in measurements on entangled particle pairs (Bell-type experiments)
measurable_quantities: correlation statistics in Bell-test experiments
claims.candidate_data: Published loophole-free Bell-test datasets constrain hidden-variable models but do not directly test the proposed network-thread mechanism.

claims.label: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs
claims.claim: The basic mechanisms underlying human perception and scientific analysis, like the mechanisms behind many natural processes, can be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
claims.quote: the evidence we have suggests that the basic mechanisms at work can once again successfully be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
claims.scope: human perception and methods of mathematical, statistical and computational analysis
measurable_quantities: accuracy with which simple-program models reproduce human perceptual judgments
algorithmic size of standard analysis procedures
claims.candidate_data: Published psychophysics and visual-neuroscience datasets on feature detection, together with open-source implementations of standard compression and statistical procedures.

claims.label: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard
claims.claim: Although inferring the generating procedure from observed behavior is fairly easy for the rules of traditional mathematics, for general simple programs it is often extremely difficult, because their complex output shows no obvious trace of its simple origin.
claims.quote: But for the more general rules that I discuss in this book it appears to often be extremely difficult. For even though the rules may be simple, the behavior they produce is often highly complex, and shows absolutely no obvious trace of its simple origins.
claims.scope: inference of generating rules from the output of cellular automata and other simple programs
measurable_quantities: success rate of rule-inference or program-synthesis methods given only final patterns
computational cost of identifying the generating rule
claims.candidate_data: Patterns generated with public cellular automaton software (e.g. Wolfram Language or Golly) used as benchmarks for existing program-synthesis and system-identification methods.

claims.label: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions
claims.claim: Defining something as random only when no short description of it exists at all is too restrictive and uncomputable (it would mean deterministic rules can never generate randomness), so any useful definition of randomness must refer to how short descriptions are to be found.
claims.quote: Indeed, what I suspect is that ultimately no useful definition of randomness can be based solely on the issue of what short descriptions of something may in principle exist.
claims.scope: definitions of randomness, including description-length (algorithmic) definitions
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Something is random if essentially no simple program detects regularities in it
claims.claim: Since essentially all standard methods of perception and analysis are based on simple programs, something should be considered random whenever essentially no simple program succeeds in detecting regularities in it.
claims.quote: something should be considered to be random whenever there is essentially no simple program that can succeed in detecting regularities in it.
claims.scope: the definition of randomness for data of any kind
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do
claims.claim: Once a few simple programs corresponding to standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities in some data, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed, so the everyday judgment of randomness is in practice fairly unambiguous.
claims.quote: For once a few simple programs corresponding to a few standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed in detecting them.
claims.scope: detection of regularities in sequences and images by simple programs
measurable_quantities: fraction of data sets passing a few standard tests that are later failed by other tests
agreement between independent randomness tests
claims.candidate_data: Public randomness test batteries such as the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite, TestU01 and Dieharder applied to many sequences.

claims.label: Complexity means our perception and analysis fail to find a short description
claims.claim: To call something complex is to say that our methods of perception and analysis have failed to find a short description of the features of it that we are interested in; complexity therefore depends on which features one chooses to capture.
claims.quote: when we say that something seems complex, what we are effectively saying is that our powers of perception and analysis have failed on it.
claims.scope: the definition of complexity
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features
claims.claim: People tend to lose interest in images with no simple features (such as perfectly random ones), and the images that hold attention and seem most aesthetically pleasing are those in which some features are simple to describe while others have no short description findable by human visual perception.
claims.quote: the images that draw us in the most—and typically that we find the most aesthetically pleasing—are those for which some features are simple for us to describe, but others have no short description that can be found by any of our standard processes of visual perception.
claims.scope: human visual attention and aesthetic preference for images
measurable_quantities: aesthetic ratings or viewing/fixation times versus compressibility of global and local image features
claims.candidate_data: Published eye-tracking and image aesthetic-rating datasets (e.g. AVA aesthetic visual analysis dataset), combined with compression-based complexity measures.

claims.label: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else
claims.claim: Structurally different lossless data compression methods (run-length, block/Huffman, pointer-based and two-dimensional schemes) have remarkably similar capabilities: they compress uniform regions, repetitive behavior and to some extent nested behavior, but achieve no substantial compression of more complex behavior even when it is generated by very short programs.
claims.quote: Essentially every method, for example, will successfully compress large regions of uniform color. And most methods manage to compress behavior that is repetitive, and at least to some extent behavior that is nested—exactly the two kinds of simple behavior that we have noted many times in this book.
claims.scope: lossless data compression algorithms applied to patterns from simple programs
measurable_quantities: compression ratios of standard compressors on uniform, repetitive, nested and complex cellular automaton patterns
claims.candidate_data: Standard open-source compressors (gzip, bzip2, xz/LZMA, zstd) applied to cellular automaton patterns generated with public software.

claims.label: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression
claims.claim: Under lossy compression by keeping only some basic forms (as in JPEG-like schemes), the relevant features of both simple and completely random images remain recognizable at high compression, whereas images normally considered complex need much lower compression, and reordering the basic forms does not change this substantially.
claims.quote: But images that one would normally consider complex tend to have features that cannot be recognized except at significantly lower levels of compression.
claims.scope: lossy transform-based image compression of simple, random and complex images
measurable_quantities: fraction of transform coefficients needed for feature recognition
perceptual quality versus compression rate by image class
claims.candidate_data: Public image collections (e.g. Kodak image set, USC-SIPI image database) and open JPEG/Walsh–Hadamard transform implementations, together with perceptual-quality measures.

claims.label: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features
claims.claim: Human perception generally works by cells responding to specific fixed features and ignoring others; in vision, cortical cells act as templates for small local patterns, and textures are distinguished by the densities of such local features, much as colors are distinguished by densities of red, green and blue.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that it is density differences such as these that allow our visual system to distinguish textures.
claims.scope: human visual texture perception
measurable_quantities: texture discrimination performance versus differences in local 2×2 block statistics at equal overall density
claims.candidate_data: Published psychophysical texture-discrimination studies and texture image databases (e.g. Brodatz textures), plus primary visual cortex receptive-field recordings.

claims.label: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting
claims.claim: Humans can readily see by eye that a two-dimensional pattern is purely repetitive, but generally cannot tell that a pattern is nested (unless it is dominated by large uniform areas), even though a simple two-dimensional pointer-based encoding recognizes the nesting.
claims.quote: it is remarkably difficult for us to tell that the patterns are nested. And this can be viewed as a clear example of a limitation in our powers of visual perception.
claims.scope: human visual recognition of repetitive and nested two-dimensional patterns
measurable_quantities: accuracy of human observers classifying patterns as repetitive, nested or random
claims.candidate_data: Psychophysics experiments using patterns from two-dimensional substitution systems generated with public software.

claims.label: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else
claims.claim: For sounds generated from sequences with fairly uniform properties, the human auditory system recognizes only exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies; nested or other non-repetitive structure, beyond a few large spectral peaks, is heard as random noise.
claims.quote: we readily recognize exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies, and essentially nothing else.
claims.scope: human auditory perception of sounds generated from discrete sequences
measurable_quantities: listener discrimination of nested versus random sequence sonifications
number of spectral peaks at which tones are no longer heard
claims.candidate_data: Auditory psychophysics experiments using sonified substitution-system sequences; existing literature on pitch perception and auditory masking.

claims.label: Best-fit probabilistic models of deterministic data look more random than the data
claims.claim: When probabilistic models such as block-frequency, Markov or probabilistic cellular automaton models are fitted to data generated by deterministic cellular automata, they reproduce the statistics used in fitting but their typical behavior is considerably more random and misses most detailed features of the data.
claims.quote: In most cases, the typical behavior produced by the model looks considerably more random than the data.
claims.scope: statistical modeling of data generated by deterministic simple programs
measurable_quantities: discrepancies in higher-order statistics and visible structure between data and samples from fitted models
claims.candidate_data: Cellular automaton data generated with public software and fitted with standard statistical packages for Markov and hidden Markov models.

claims.label: Equal block frequencies of all lengths is not a universal randomness test
claims.claim: Checking that all blocks of all lengths occur with equal frequency does not guarantee absence of regularity: sequences such as linear feedback shift register output or concatenated binary digits of successive integers have accurate block frequencies yet are non-random, as revealed for instance by an abnormally small spread of those frequencies.
claims.quote: it has sometimes been thought that if one could just compute frequencies of blocks of all lengths one would have a kind of universal test for randomness. But sequences like (e) and (f) on the facing page make it clear that this is not the case.
claims.scope: block-frequency tests for randomness of binary sequences
measurable_quantities: block frequencies and their variance for LFSR and Champernowne-type binary sequences versus random sequences
claims.candidate_data: Sequences computable with standard tools; the binary Champernowne sequence is catalogued in the OEIS.

claims.label: Rule 30 center column and digits of pi pass statistical tests for randomness
claims.claim: The center column of the rule 30 cellular automaton and the base 2 digits of pi show no detectable deviation from randomness under block-frequency statistics or under analysis by simple cellular automata, even though both are generated by simple rules.
claims.quote: statistical analysis, even with some generalization, cannot readily recognize that sequences like (g) and (h) are anything but completely random—even though at an underlying level these sequences were generated by quite simple rules.
claims.scope: the rule 30 center-column sequence and the binary expansion of pi
measurable_quantities: p-values from standard randomness test batteries
block-frequency deviations relative to random sequences
claims.candidate_data: Rule 30 center column (catalogued in the OEIS) and published high-precision digits of pi, tested with NIST SP 800-22, TestU01 or Dieharder.

claims.label: Rule 30 can serve as a cryptographic stream cipher as secure as any known
claims.claim: Simple rules with complex behavior, such as the rule 30 cellular automaton sampled sparsely to give an encrypting sequence, can be used to build stream ciphers at least as secure against cryptanalysis as any known system, unlike additive cellular automata or linear feedback shift registers, whose keys are easily recovered.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that they can, and that in fact they allow one to construct systems that are at least as secure to cryptanalysis as any that are known.
claims.scope: stream ciphers based on cellular automata, specifically rule 30
measurable_quantities: computational cost of key recovery from known keystream for rule 30 ciphers versus established ciphers
claims.candidate_data: Published cryptanalysis literature on cellular automaton stream ciphers and standard cryptographic test suites.

claims.label: Every nested pattern likely has a formula in generalized hypergeometric functions
claims.claim: Although most nested patterns have no obvious relation to ordinary mathematical functions, a formula for the color of each cell of any nested pattern can probably be found in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions or similar generalizations of traditional functions.
claims.quote: it is my guess that in the end it will in fact turn out to be possible to get a formula for any nested pattern in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions
claims.scope: nested patterns generated by substitution systems
measurable_quantities: existence of closed-form hypergeometric expressions for cell colors of specific nested patterns
claims.candidate_data: Computer algebra systems and the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions for hypergeometric identities.

claims.label: No simple formula describes many steps of rule 30 evolution
claims.claim: Minimal Boolean formulas (in disjunctive normal form or in Nand operations) for the outcome of rule 30 grow rapidly with the number of steps, unlike those for simple rules such as 90 and 254, indicating that no simple formula describes rule 30 evolution and that, in most cases, cellular automaton patterns have no simple mathematical formula.
claims.quote: So even if one allows rather general structure, the evidence is that in the end there is no way to set up any simple formula that will describe the outcome of evolution for a system like rule 30.
claims.scope: formula representations of cellular automaton evolution, especially rule 30
measurable_quantities: number of terms in minimal DNF expressions per step
minimal Nand circuit size per step
claims.candidate_data: Boolean minimization tools (e.g. Espresso logic minimizer) and SAT-based exact circuit synthesis applied to rule 30.

claims.label: Human memory works like similarity-preserving hashing by layers of neurons
claims.claim: Human memory likely retrieves data by a simple hashing-like mechanism in which successive layers of nerve cells, each responding to patterns in fixed random sets of inputs, produce representations that are the same for inputs differing by small changes, allowing retrieval by similarity.
claims.quote: this basic mechanism provides a simple way to get a representation—and thus a hash code—that will tend to be the same for pieces of data that somehow have enough features that are similar.
claims.scope: mechanisms of human memory storage and retrieval
measurable_quantities: invariance of neural population responses to small input changes
similarity-based recall performance
claims.candidate_data: Neurophysiological recordings of sensory and hippocampal neurons (e.g. Allen Brain Observatory) and work on locality-sensitive hashing in olfactory circuits.

claims.label: Memory retrieval, not logic, underlies almost all of human thinking
claims.claim: Retrieval from memory on the basis of similarity underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking, including generalization, analogy and intuition, and logical reasoning is not fundamental but is itself carried out by retrieving learned patterns of argument from memory.
claims.quote: My strong suspicion is that the use of memory is what in fact underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking.
claims.scope: human cognition
measurable_quantities: dependence of reasoning performance on familiarity with argument patterns
speed of memory retrieval versus stepwise reasoning
claims.candidate_data: Published cognitive psychology studies of content effects in reasoning (e.g. Wason selection task) and analogical retrieval.

claims.label: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules
claims.claim: Despite the complicated construction of the brain, there is a core to human thinking that is largely independent of neural details and is based on rather simple rules, with nothing fundamentally special about the processes involved.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that there is a definite core to the phenomenon of human thinking that is largely independent of such details—and that will in the end turn out to be based on rules that are rather simple.
claims.scope: human thinking and its emulation by artificial systems
measurable_quantities: size of the simplest systems that emulate general human-like thinking
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: General human-like thinking is easier to reproduce than task-specific versions
claims.claim: Because complex behavior from simple rules is hard to direct to specific tasks, it will likely be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than a special version of human-like thinking restricted to specific tasks; a recognizably human-like system would also need a human-like base of experience.
claims.quote: most likely it will at some level be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than to set up some special version of human-like thinking only for specific tasks.
claims.scope: artificial intelligence and emulation of human thinking
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Higher Forms of Perception and Analysis
claims.label: No method of perception or analysis can recognize all possible regularities
claims.claim: No method of perception and analysis, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize all possible regularities and thus tell immediately whether a piece of data can be generated from some simple description, although higher methods could recognize some regularities current methods miss.
claims.quote: My strong belief—as I will argue in Chapter 12—is that at least in complete generality this will never be possible.
claims.scope: all possible methods of perception and analysis
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Higher Forms of Perception and Analysis
claims.label: Practical perception and analysis methods recognize only repetition and nesting
claims.claim: Essentially all methods of perception and analysis in practical use have similar capabilities, recognizing repetition and sometimes nesting but almost nothing more complex, possibly because only such regularities are both common and quickly recognizable, or because humans choose methods matching their built-in perception.
claims.quote: Most of them, for example, recognize repetition, and some also recognize nesting. But almost none recognize anything more complex.
claims.scope: human perception and standard methods of mathematical, statistical and computational analysis
measurable_quantities: performance of standard analysis methods on repetitive, nested and more complex generated data
claims.candidate_data: Standard compressors and statistical test suites applied to benchmark sets of patterns generated by simple programs.

claims.section: Higher Forms of Perception and Analysis
claims.label: Extraterrestrial signals taken for noise could be meaningful messages
claims.claim: Some extraterrestrial radio and other signals that are detected and assumed to be random noise could be meaningful messages encoded in a way recognizable only by higher forms of perception and analysis than those applied so far.
claims.quote: it seems far from inconceivable that some of the extraterrestrial radio and other signals that we pick up and assume to be random noise could in fact be meaningful messages
claims.scope: astronomical radio and other signals searched for extraterrestrial intelligence
measurable_quantities: compressibility or detectable algorithmic structure in signals classified as noise
claims.candidate_data: Breakthrough Listen open data archive of radio observations.

claims.label: Computation is the central organizing idea of the new science
claims.claim: The most important idea underlying Wolfram's new kind of science is computation: systems such as cellular automata should be viewed as computations, with initial conditions as input and later states as output, so that systems with entirely different rules can be discussed in a unified, abstract way.
claims.quote: And in many respects the single most important idea that underlies this new science is the notion of computation.
claims.scope: the methodology of the new kind of science; cellular automata and other simple programs
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Any system can be viewed as performing a computation
claims.claim: Any system whatsoever, not just a cellular automaton, can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.
claims.quote: At some level, any cellular automaton—or for that matter, any system whatsoever—can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.
claims.scope: all systems, natural or artificial
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Universality is crucial for understanding complexity in natural systems
claims.claim: Although universality has never before been seriously considered in natural science, it is crucial for finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity seen in natural systems.
claims.quote: But what I will show in this chapter and the next is that in fact universality is for example quite crucial in finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity we see in natural systems.
claims.scope: natural systems exhibiting complex behavior
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: A universal system can produce arbitrarily complex behavior
claims.claim: Because a universal system can emulate any other system, it can produce behavior as complex as that of any other system, so knowing a system is universal implies it can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.
claims.quote: So knowing that a particular system is universal thus immediately implies that the system can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.
claims.scope: universal computational systems of any kind
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Universality is widespread and occurs in many systems in nature
claims.claim: Contrary to the assumption that universality is rare and found only in systems specifically constructed to have it, universality is a widespread phenomenon that also occurs in a wide range of important systems found in nature.
claims.quote: But one of the results of this chapter is that in fact universality is a much more widespread phenomenon. And in the next chapter I will argue that for example it also occurs in a wide range of important systems that we see in nature.
claims.scope: computational and natural systems in general
measurable_quantities: fraction of systems of a given type that can be proved universal
claims.candidate_data: Published catalogs of proven-universal small Turing machines, cellular automata and tag systems bear on the computational part; no data resource is known for natural systems.

claims.label: A fixed universal cellular automaton can emulate any cellular automaton
claims.claim: A single cellular automaton with fixed rules (Wolfram's 19-color, next-nearest-neighbor construction) can, given suitable initial conditions, emulate any cellular automaton whatsoever, regardless of how many colors or neighbors its rules involve, including rules more complicated than its own.
claims.quote: And the conclusion is therefore that the universal cellular automaton can ultimately emulate a cellular automaton with absolutely any set of rules, regardless of how many neighbors and how many colors they may involve.
claims.scope: one-dimensional cellular automata with any number of colors and any neighborhood size
measurable_quantities: correctness of the block-encoded emulation of target rules over many steps
emulation overhead in steps per emulated step
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of the published rule with Wolfram Language or other cellular automaton software can check the emulations.

claims.section: Emulating Other Systems with Cellular Automata
claims.label: Cellular automata can emulate nearly all other system types, even computers
claims.claim: Cellular automata can be set up to emulate almost every type of system considered in the book—mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, sequential substitution and tag systems, register machines, arithmetic systems, logic circuits and random-access memory—and in principle a practical computer in its entirety.
claims.quote: But what I will show in this section is that in fact this is not the case, and that in the end cellular automata can actually be made to emulate almost every single type of system that we have discussed in this book.
claims.scope: cellular automata versus mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, register machines, arithmetic systems and practical computers
measurable_quantities: existence and correctness of explicit cellular automaton emulations for each system type
claims.candidate_data: Explicit constructions can be verified by simulation with Wolfram Language or open-source cellular automaton simulators.

claims.section: Emulating Other Systems with Cellular Automata
claims.label: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step
claims.claim: Unlike mobile automata or Turing machines, substitution systems cannot in general be emulated one step per cellular automaton step, because the number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor each step while a cellular automaton pattern can grow only by a fixed amount per step; progressively more cellular automaton steps are needed per substitution step.
claims.quote: That this must ultimately be the case one can see from the fact that the total number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor from one step to the next, while in a cellular automaton the size of a pattern can only ever increase by a fixed amount at each step.
claims.scope: cellular automaton emulation of substitution systems
measurable_quantities: growth rate of pattern size per step in substitution systems versus cellular automata
claims.candidate_data: Follows from elementary arguments and can be checked by simulation with standard software.

claims.section: Emulating Cellular Automata with Other Systems
claims.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata
claims.claim: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only generate repetitive or nested patterns, so they cannot emulate cellular automata such as rule 30, whereas neighbor-dependent substitution systems can emulate cellular automata straightforwardly.
claims.quote: For as we discussed on page 83, neighbor-independent substitution systems can generate only patterns that are either repetitive or nested—so they can never yield the more complicated patterns that are, for example, needed to emulate rule 30.
claims.scope: neighbor-independent and neighbor-dependent substitution systems
measurable_quantities: whether patterns generated by neighbor-independent substitution systems are always repetitive or nested
claims.candidate_data: Theory of morphic and automatic sequences, and direct enumeration of substitution rules with standard software, bear on it.

claims.section: Emulating Cellular Automata with Other Systems
claims.label: Any system type that can emulate every cellular automaton has universal members
claims.claim: Since a universal cellular automaton exists, any type of system shown capable of emulating any cellular automaton—including mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbor-dependent and sequential substitution systems, tag systems, cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines—must contain universal examples.
claims.quote: And as soon as one knows that any particular type of system is capable of emulating any cellular automaton, it immediately follows that there must be examples of that type of system that are universal.
claims.scope: mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems, register machines
claims.candidate_data: Explicit emulation constructions can be verified by simulation with Wolfram Language or other software.

claims.section: Emulating Cellular Automata with Other Systems
claims.label: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal
claims.claim: A system that repeatedly takes a whole number, computes its remainder modulo a constant and applies an arithmetic operation chosen by that remainder can emulate a register machine, and is therefore universal; given how widespread universality is, arithmetic supporting it is unsurprising.
claims.quote: The picture below shows that such a system can be set up to emulate a register machine. And from the fact that register machines are universal it follows that so too are such arithmetic systems.
claims.scope: generalized arithmetic (Collatz-like) iteration systems
measurable_quantities: correctness of the register-machine encoding over many steps
claims.candidate_data: The construction can be verified by direct computation, and published work on generalized Collatz functions bears on it.

claims.label: Structurally different systems are computationally equivalent
claims.claim: Because essentially all the kinds of systems studied (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and others) can emulate each other, a wide variety of systems with very different underlying structures are fundamentally equivalent in the computations they can perform, so computation can be studied abstractly with results applying across systems.
claims.quote: In a sense its most important consequence is that it implies that from a computational point of view a very wide variety of systems, with very different underlying structures, are at some level fundamentally equivalent.
claims.scope: cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and other simple programs
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Past the threshold of universality, more complex rules add no capability
claims.claim: As systems of a given type are given progressively greater computational capabilities they eventually pass a threshold of universality, after which the set of computations they can perform is always the same, so more sophisticated rules gain nothing further and a universal system's capabilities are independent of the details of its construction.
claims.quote: But the phenomenon of universality implies that this is not the case, and that as soon as one has passed the threshold of universality, nothing more can in a sense ever be gained.
claims.scope: all universal systems, of any type
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Elementary cellular automaton rule 110 is universal
claims.claim: Rule 110, a two-color nearest-neighbor elementary cellular automaton, is universal: by arranging its naturally occurring localized structures as components, it can be made to emulate any cyclic tag system, and hence any Turing machine.
claims.quote: And indeed in the case of rule 110 it took several years of work to develop the necessary ideas and tools. But finally it has turned out to be possible to show that the rule 110 cellular automaton is in fact universal.
claims.scope: the rule 110 elementary cellular automaton
measurable_quantities: correctness of the cyclic tag system emulation in rule 110 simulations
claims.candidate_data: The construction can be checked by simulating rule 110 with Wolfram Language or open-source cellular automaton software; the peer-reviewed mathematical literature on rule 110 bears on the proof.

claims.section: The Significance of Universality in Rule 110
claims.label: Universality should be common, including among very simple rules
claims.claim: The universality of rule 110, one of the simplest possible cellular automaton rules, implies that universality is far more common than previously thought and should occur in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.
claims.quote: But knowing that a system like rule 110 is universal, the whole picture changes, and now it seems likely that instead universality should actually be seen in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.
claims.scope: simple programs of all kinds
measurable_quantities: fraction of small rules of each system type that are universal
claims.candidate_data: Published results on small universal Turing machines, tag systems and cellular automata, plus exhaustive enumeration of small rules with public software, bear on it.

claims.section: The Significance of Universality in Rule 110
claims.label: Complexity of behavior saturates soon after the simplest rules
claims.claim: As rules become progressively more complicated, overall behavior grows more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached, and since that threshold is very low, behavior beyond the very simplest rules of any kind should quickly become as complex as it will ever be—consistent with the Chapter 3 survey.
claims.quote: So what this means is that if one looks at a sequence of systems with progressively more complicated rules, one should expect that the overall behavior they produce will become more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached.
claims.scope: cellular automata, Turing machines and other simple programs enumerated by rule complexity
measurable_quantities: measures of behavioral complexity (e.g. compressibility, entropy) versus rule size across enumerated rule spaces
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive enumerations of small cellular automata and Turing machines run with public software, and published algorithmic-complexity studies of rule spaces, bear on it.

claims.label: All class 4 cellular automata are expected to be universal
claims.claim: Any cellular automaton showing class 4 behavior (localized structures moving and interacting in complicated ways) will, like rule 110, turn out to be universal, because such rules eventually yield localized structures rich enough to support universality.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that it is true in general that any cellular automaton which shows overall class 4 behavior will turn out—like rule 110—to be universal.
claims.scope: class 4 cellular automata
measurable_quantities: number of class 4 rules with proved universality versus those shown non-universal
claims.candidate_data: Literature on universality proofs for specific cellular automata (e.g. the Game of Life) and simulation with public software bear on it.

claims.label: Rule 110 and its reflections are the only clear elementary class 4 rules
claims.claim: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata, the only clear immediate example of class 4 behavior is rule 110 together with its left-right and black-white equivalents (rules 124, 137 and 193), while class 4 behavior is common once more colors or neighbors are allowed, even for totalistic rules.
claims.quote: Among the 256 so-called elementary cellular automata that allow only two possible colors for each cell and depend only on nearest neighbors, the only clear immediate example is rule 110—together with rules 124, 137 and 193 obtained by trivially reversing left and right or black and white.
claims.scope: the 256 elementary cellular automata and multi-color or larger-neighborhood rules
measurable_quantities: classification of all 256 elementary rules by behavior class
presence of interacting localized structures
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive simulation of the 256 elementary rules with Wolfram Language or open-source tools bears on it.

claims.section: The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata
claims.label: Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal
claims.claim: Cellular automata that produce only uniform or repetitive patterns (class 1 and class 2) can never be universal, because they transmit information only over limited distances and so support only processes involving a limited number of cells.
claims.quote: In a sense the fundamental reason for this—as we discussed on page 252—is that such class 1 and class 2 cellular automata never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances.
claims.scope: class 1 and class 2 cellular automata
measurable_quantities: maximum distance over which a single-cell perturbation spreads
claims.candidate_data: Perturbation-spreading experiments on elementary cellular automata with public simulation software bear on it.

claims.section: The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata
claims.label: Nested-pattern and additive cellular automata cannot be universal
claims.claim: Cellular automata whose information transmission is highly constrained so that patterns are essentially nested, and additive rules such as rules 90 and 150 whose states after a power-of-two number of steps are simple superpositions of shifted copies of the initial condition, cannot be universal.
claims.quote: And since there are many kinds of behavior that do not return to such predictable forms after any limited number of steps, one must conclude that additive rules cannot be universal.
claims.scope: additive and nested-pattern cellular automata, e.g. rules 90 and 150
measurable_quantities: configuration after 2^k steps compared with superpositions of shifted initial conditions
claims.candidate_data: Algebraic theory of linear cellular automata and direct simulation with public software bear on it.

claims.section: The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata
claims.label: Rule 54 shows only repetitive or nested forms in 100 million initial conditions
claims.claim: Rule 54, a possible class 4 elementary cellular automaton, shows only repetitive or nested behavior in its first hundred million initial conditions, leaving it uncertain whether rule 54 is universal.
claims.quote: And as one continues one sees various other repetitive and nested forms. But at least up to the hundred millionth initial condition one sees nothing that is fundamentally any more complicated.
claims.scope: the rule 54 elementary cellular automaton
measurable_quantities: long-term behavior classification for each initial condition up to 10^8
claims.candidate_data: Can be rechecked by exhaustive simulation with public cellular automaton software.

claims.section: The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata
claims.label: Any non-repetitive, non-nested system is expected to be universal
claims.claim: More or less any system whose behavior is not fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal, so there is a close connection between universality and the appearance of complex behavior, though proving it will be far easier for some systems (such as rule 110) than others.
claims.quote: As I will discuss in the next chapter, my general expectation is that more or less any system whose behavior is not somehow fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal.
claims.scope: all systems showing complex (non-repetitive, non-nested) behavior
measurable_quantities: proportion of complex-behaving small rules for which universality has been proved
claims.candidate_data: Published universality results for small Turing machines, cellular automata and tag systems bear on it.

claims.section: The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata
claims.label: Uncontrolled information flow in class 3 rules hinders universality proofs
claims.claim: Universality proofs proceed by building components from localized structures, which requires controlled transmission of information; in class 3 systems a change to a single cell eventually spreads to all cells, making it very hard to identify definite components and hence to prove universality.
claims.quote: And this kind of uncontrolled transmission of information makes it very difficult to identify pieces that could be used as definite components in a construction.
claims.scope: class 3 cellular automata and methods for proving universality
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata
claims.label: Rules 30 and 45 are expected to be universal
claims.claim: Although the localized structures found in rules 30 and 45 on repetitive backgrounds all move at the same speed and so cannot interact, preventing a rule 110-style proof, rules 30 and 45 will nevertheless turn out to be universal.
claims.quote: So although this means that the particular type of approach we used to demonstrate the universality of rule 110 cannot immediately be used for rule 30 or rule 45, it certainly does not mean that these rules are not in the end universal.
claims.scope: the rule 30 and rule 45 elementary cellular automata
measurable_quantities: existence of universality constructions for rules 30 and 45
velocities of localized structures on repetitive backgrounds
claims.candidate_data: Searches for localized structures with public cellular automaton software bear on part of it; no data settles universality.

claims.section: The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata
claims.label: Complex elementary rules can emulate one step of every elementary rule
claims.claim: Using block encodings, elementary rules with complex behavior such as rules 22, 30 and 110 can be made to emulate a single step of all 256 elementary cellular automata, whereas rules with simple behavior such as 90 and 184 can emulate only a few; this supports the idea that complex-looking cellular automata can do arbitrarily sophisticated computations.
claims.quote: But for underlying rules that have more complex behavior—like rules 22, 30, or 110—it turns out that in the end it is always possible to emulate all 256 elementary rules.
claims.scope: single-step block emulation among the 256 elementary cellular automata
measurable_quantities: number of elementary rules emulable for one step as a function of block width
claims.candidate_data: Can be recomputed by exhaustive search with public cellular automaton software.

claims.section: The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata
claims.label: Perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal
claims.claim: Since elementary cellular automata whose behavior looks complex can do computations as sophisticated as desired, they are expected to be universal, so perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal.
claims.quote: And this suggests that such cellular automata will in the end turn out to be universal—with the result that out of the 256 elementary rules one expects that perhaps as many as 27 will in fact be universal.
claims.scope: the 256 elementary cellular automata
measurable_quantities: number of elementary rules proved universal or proved non-universal
claims.candidate_data: Published mathematical results on universality and non-universality of specific elementary cellular automata bear on it.

claims.section: Universality in Turing Machines and Other Systems
claims.label: A 2-state 5-color Turing machine is universal via rule 110
claims.claim: A Turing machine with just 2 states and 5 colors, far simpler than the 7-state 4-color machine that had long been the simplest known, is universal because it emulates rule 110 by sweeping back and forth and updating all cells by one rule 110 step per sweep.
claims.quote: And in fact, by using the universality of rule 110 it turns out to be possible to come up with the vastly simpler universal Turing machine shown below—with just 2 states and 5 possible colors.
claims.scope: small universal Turing machines
measurable_quantities: correctness of the rule 110 emulation by the 2-state 5-color machine
claims.candidate_data: The machine can be simulated against rule 110 with Wolfram Language or any Turing machine simulator.

claims.section: Universality in Turing Machines and Other Systems
claims.label: No 2-state 2-color Turing machine can be universal
claims.claim: All 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors have behavior too simple to support universality.
claims.quote: If one looks at the 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors it is fairly easy to see that their behavior is in all cases too simple to support universality.
claims.scope: 2-state 2-color Turing machines
measurable_quantities: behavior classification of all 4096 machines
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive enumeration with public Turing machine simulators bears on it.

claims.section: Universality in Turing Machines and Other Systems
claims.label: Complex behavior is rare but present in small Turing machine spaces
claims.claim: Starting from a blank tape, roughly one in 50,000 2-state 4-color Turing machines and one in 200,000 4-state 2-color machines show complex behavior, and 14 essentially equivalent machines among the 2,985,984 with 2 states and 3 colors do so.
claims.quote: Among such 2-state 4-color Turing machines perhaps one in 50,000 shows complex behavior when started from a blank tape.
claims.scope: 2-state 4-color, 4-state 2-color and 2-state 3-color Turing machines
measurable_quantities: fraction of machines in each rule space with complex behavior from blank tape
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive enumeration of the rule spaces with public Turing machine simulators bears on it.

claims.section: Universality in Turing Machines and Other Systems
claims.label: A complex 2-state 3-color Turing machine is likely the simplest universal one
claims.claim: The 2-state 3-color Turing machine numbered 596,440, which yields complicated behavior from a blank tape, is likely universal, and if so would by most measures be the simplest universal Turing machine.
claims.quote: And although it will no doubt be very difficult to prove, it seems likely that this Turing machine will in the end turn out to be universal. And if so, then presumably it will by most measures be the very simplest Turing machine that is universal.
claims.scope: 2-state 3-color Turing machines
measurable_quantities: existence of a universality proof for the machine
claims.candidate_data: The machine's behavior can be simulated with public software; universality is a question for mathematical proof.

claims.section: Universality in Turing Machines and Other Systems
claims.label: All 3-state 2-color Turing machines behave simply from blank tape
claims.claim: With blank initial conditions all 2,985,984 Turing machines with 3 states and 2 colors quickly produce simple repetitive or nested behavior, and even with more complicated initial conditions their behavior eventually seems to resolve into a simple form.
claims.quote: With 3 states and 2 colors it turns out that with blank initial conditions all of the 2,985,984 possible Turing machines of this type quickly evolve to produce simple repetitive or nested behavior.
claims.scope: 3-state 2-color Turing machines
measurable_quantities: behavior classification of each machine from blank tape
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive enumeration with public Turing machine simulators bears on it.

claims.section: Universality in Turing Machines and Other Systems
claims.label: Combinators show highly complex behavior despite simple rules
claims.claim: Combinators, symbolic systems long known to be universal, show highly complex behavior despite simple rules—for example a length-8 initial expression grows exponentially with seemingly random internal structure—and they can emulate rule 110, suggesting their universality is just associated with general complex behavior.
claims.quote: But from pictures like the ones on the facing page it is rather clear that despite their fairly simple underlying rules, the behavior of combinators can be highly complex.
claims.scope: S and K combinator systems
measurable_quantities: expression size versus evolution step for short initial expressions
claims.candidate_data: Can be recomputed by enumerating short combinator expressions with Wolfram Language or other term-rewriting software.

claims.label: Every process, natural or artificial, can be viewed as a computation
claims.claim: Any process that follows definite rules, including processes in nature governed by physical law as well as processes constructed by humans, can be viewed as a computation, giving a uniform framework for comparing very different processes.
claims.quote: all processes, whether they are produced by human effort or occur spontaneously in nature, can be viewed as computations.
claims.scope: all natural and artificial processes
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Principle of Computational Equivalence: one maximal level of sophistication
claims.claim: Almost all processes whose behavior is not obviously simple correspond to computations of equivalent sophistication; there is essentially a single highest level of computational sophistication, and almost all such processes reach it regardless of how simple their rules or initial conditions are.
claims.quote: the most general is just to say that almost all processes that are not obviously simple can be viewed as computations of equivalent sophistication.
claims.scope: essentially all processes in nature, mathematics and engineered systems whose behavior is not obviously simple
measurable_quantities: fraction of non-simple rules in an enumerated class proven universal
computational equivalence (mutual emulability) of processes
claims.candidate_data: Exhaustive enumerations of elementary and totalistic cellular automata and small Turing machines run with Wolfram Language or other open simulators, together with the published literature on universality proofs.

claims.label: No physical system can compute beyond cellular automata and Turing machines
claims.claim: As a law of nature, no system that can actually be constructed in our universe can carry out explicit computations more sophisticated than those of universal systems such as cellular automata and Turing machines; imaginable hypercomputers (e.g. with infinite tables of results) cannot be built.
claims.quote: no system can ever carry out explicit computations that are more sophisticated than those carried out by systems like cellular automata and Turing machines.
claims.scope: all physical systems in our universe, including computers and brains
measurable_quantities: existence of any physical device that decides a Turing-undecidable problem
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: An overwhelming fraction of non-simple rules are universal
claims.claim: Among all possible rules of a given type (such as cellular automata) whose behavior is not obviously simple, i.e. not repetitive or nested, the overwhelming majority are computationally universal, so universality is extremely common rather than a rare engineered property.
claims.quote: among all possible systems with behavior that is not obviously simple an overwhelming fraction are universal.
claims.scope: enumerable classes of simple programs such as cellular automata, Turing machines and related systems
measurable_quantities: number of rules in a class with non-repetitive, non-nested behavior
number of those rules proven universal or proven non-universal
claims.candidate_data: Enumerations of elementary and small totalistic cellular automata and small Turing machines, compared against published universality proofs such as that for rule 110.

claims.label: Rules occurring in nature are typically not specially selected
claims.claim: When no constraint such as engineering design or natural selection forces simple behavior, the rules that operate in nature are effectively selected in no special way apart from tending to be structurally simple, so they behave like randomly chosen rules and are almost always universal when their behavior is not obviously simple.
claims.quote: most rules that appear in nature can be viewed as being selected in no special way—save perhaps for the fact that the structure of the rules themselves tends to be fairly simple.
claims.scope: rules governing natural systems not constrained by engineering or natural selection
measurable_quantities: statistical properties of rules inferred for natural systems compared with random rule ensembles
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Rule 30 from a single cell contains every possible block
claims.claim: The pattern generated by the rule 30 cellular automaton from a single black cell appears to contain every possible block of cells eventually, so that essentially any possible computation exists somewhere within this single pattern.
claims.quote: So far as I can tell, all possible blocks eventually appear, potentially letting the pattern serve as a kind of directory of all possible computations.
claims.scope: rule 30 elementary cellular automaton started from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: for each block length k, the number of distinct length-k blocks occurring in the first t steps
step at which each block first appears
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 30 with Wolfram Language or open-source cellular automaton code; OEIS entries on the rule 30 pattern and center column.

claims.label: Complicated molecules generally do not reach minimum-energy configurations
claims.claim: Although simple molecules may settle into minimum-energy configurations, complicated molecules typically do not; they explore configurations by an explicit evolution process, so nature does not actually solve hard constraint-satisfaction problems as traditional models idealize.
claims.quote: while in simple cases complicated molecules may for example arrange themselves in configurations that minimize energy, the evidence is that in more complicated cases they typically do not.
claims.scope: molecular configurations such as large biomolecules and glasses
measurable_quantities: energy of observed molecular conformations relative to computed global minima
occurrence of kinetically trapped or metastable states
claims.candidate_data: Protein Data Bank structures compared with energy-minimization and folding-simulation results, and published studies of glassy and metastable molecular states.

claims.label: Continuous systems cannot exceed discrete computation in practice
claims.claim: Continuous systems, including analog computers, systems described by continuous equations, and even idealized perfectly continuous systems under reasonable assumptions, cannot perform computations fundamentally more sophisticated than discrete systems like cellular automata; continuity is largely an idealization.
claims.quote: even idealized perfectly continuous systems will never in fact be able to perform fundamentally more sophisticated computations.
claims.scope: analog computers, continuous mathematical models, and physical systems treated as continuous
measurable_quantities: computational power of analog devices relative to digital computers
precision and noise limits in analog computation
claims.candidate_data: Published literature on analog computation and real-number models of computation; no specific dataset known.

claims.label: Equations with trigonometric functions can encode infinite computations
claims.claim: Whereas solving pure polynomial equations allows no computation beyond that of ordinary discrete systems, once trigonometric functions are allowed one can construct equations whose solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of infinitely many steps of a system like a cellular automaton.
claims.quote: as soon as one even allows trigonometric functions, for example, it turns out that it becomes possible to construct equations for which finding a solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of an infinite number of steps in the evolution of a system like a cellular automaton.
claims.scope: equations built from standard mathematical functions
claims.candidate_data: Published results in mathematical logic on decidability of equations over the reals with trigonometric functions.

claims.label: Human thinking rests on rather simple computational processes
claims.claim: The basic mechanisms of human thinking will turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes, so human thought does not perform computations beyond the level allowed by the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
claims.quote: the basic mechanisms of human thinking will in the end turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes.
claims.scope: human brains and thinking
measurable_quantities: complexity of mechanistic models needed to reproduce human cognitive behavior
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: No hidden regularity beyond repetition and nesting in rule-30-like systems
claims.claim: There is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems with complex behavior such as rule 30; beyond systems with obvious regularities like repetition and nesting, most systems are universal and computationally equivalent.
claims.quote: I have gradually come to the conclusion that there is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems, and that instead what the Principle of Computational Equivalence suggests is correct
claims.scope: simple programs with non-repetitive, non-nested behavior, such as rule 30
measurable_quantities: statistical randomness test results on rule 30 output
success of compression or prediction methods on such patterns
universality status of rule 30
claims.candidate_data: Rule 30 center-column sequences (OEIS) analyzed with standard randomness test suites such as NIST SP 800-22 or TestU01.

claims.label: Complexity arises because observers are computationally equivalent to systems
claims.claim: Systems with simple rules appear complex because, once a low threshold is passed, their evolution is as computationally sophisticated as any process of perception or analysis used to study them, and this holds for any method of perception and analysis that can actually be used.
claims.quote: observers will tend to be computationally equivalent to the systems they observe—with the inevitable consequence that they will consider the behavior of such systems complex.
claims.scope: observers (human or otherwise) studying systems in nature and simple programs
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Computational irreducibility blocks shortcuts to predicting behavior
claims.claim: For computationally irreducible systems, even with complete knowledge of rules and initial conditions, there is no way to predict the behavior except by performing almost as many computational steps as the system's own evolution.
claims.quote: there can be no way to predict how the system will behave except by going through almost as many steps of computation as the evolution of the system itself.
claims.scope: any system whose evolution is computationally irreducible
measurable_quantities: computational cost of the fastest known method to obtain the state after t steps, as a function of t
claims.candidate_data: Benchmarks of algorithms for computing cellular automaton states after t steps (e.g. rule 30 center column) using open simulation tools.

claims.label: Only obviously simple behavior is reducible; nearly all else is irreducible
claims.claim: Behavior that is obviously simple, such as repetitive or nested behavior, is always computationally reducible, while in practically all other cases behavior is computationally irreducible.
claims.quote: If the behavior of a system is obviously simple—and is say either repetitive or nested—then it will always be computationally reducible. But it follows from the Principle of Computational Equivalence that in practically all other cases it will be computationally irreducible.
claims.scope: all systems, especially simple programs
measurable_quantities: existence of sub-linear-time procedures for computing states of repetitive, nested and other cellular automata
claims.candidate_data: Enumerations of elementary cellular automata classified by behavior, with known closed-form or fast algorithms for additive and nested rules.

claims.label: Traditional theoretical science fails where irreducibility is present
claims.claim: Traditional theoretical science, including its use of mathematical formulas, relies on computational reducibility, which is the fundamental reason it has made little progress with systems whose behavior is not quite simple and why it has tended to restrict its domain to reducible phenomena.
claims.quote: this, I believe, is the fundamental reason that traditional theoretical science has never managed to get far in studying most types of systems whose behavior is not ultimately quite simple.
claims.scope: theoretical science and mathematical modeling
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Many common systems can only be understood by explicit simulation
claims.claim: Computer simulation is not merely a convenient substitute for mathematical formulas: there are many common systems whose behavior can be determined only by something like explicit simulation, and there can be no easy theory for almost any behavior that seems complex.
claims.quote: there are many common systems whose behavior cannot in the end be determined at all except by something like an explicit simulation.
claims.scope: common natural and artificial systems with complex behavior
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Nested cellular automaton patterns can be computed in logarithmic time
claims.claim: For cellular automata with nested behavior such as elementary rules 60 and 188, the color of a cell after t steps can be found in about log2(t) steps from the base-2 digits of its position, rather than by tracing all t steps.
claims.quote: In general, to find the color of a cell after t steps of rule 188 or rule 60 evolution takes about Log[2, t] steps.
claims.scope: elementary cellular automata rules 60 and 188, and nested patterns generally
measurable_quantities: steps needed to compute cell color at step t
agreement with direct simulation
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of rules 60 and 188 alongside digit-based fast procedures (e.g. Lucas's theorem for rule 60) using open tools.

claims.label: Complex-looking yet computationally reducible systems are very rare
claims.claim: Systems whose behavior looks complex but is nevertheless computationally reducible, such as the cellular automaton that generates digits of powers of 2, are very rare; in the vast majority of cases complex-looking behavior in nature and elsewhere is computationally irreducible.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that systems like this are very rare, and that in the vast majority of cases where the behavior that we see in nature and elsewhere appears to us complex it is in the end indeed associated with computational irreducibility.
claims.scope: systems with complex-looking behavior in nature and among simple programs
measurable_quantities: fraction of complex-looking rules in an enumerated class for which a fast (polylog or sub-linear) evaluation procedure exists
claims.candidate_data: Enumerations of small cellular automata searched for fast evaluation procedures using open simulation tools.

claims.label: Apparent free will stems from irreducible brain computation
claims.claim: The apparent freedom of human will arises because, although brain components follow definite laws, the brain's overall behavior is an irreducible computation whose outcome cannot be found by reasonable laws; no external influence, chaos, or quantum randomness is needed.
claims.quote: even though all the components of our brains presumably follow definite laws, I strongly suspect that their overall behavior corresponds to an irreducible computation whose outcome can never in effect be found by reasonable laws.
claims.scope: human brains and other systems that appear to exhibit free will
measurable_quantities: predictability of decisions from neural measurements
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Undecidability shows up with very simple rules and initial conditions
claims.claim: Undecidability has obvious effects even in a very simple system: in a 4-color totalistic cellular automaton (code 1004600) started from simple initial conditions, some patterns die out only after over a thousand steps while others are still growing after ten million steps with no indication of their final outcome.
claims.quote: undecidability can have quite obvious effects even with a very simple underlying rule and very simple initial conditions.
claims.scope: 4-color totalistic cellular automaton with code 1004600 and simple programs generally
measurable_quantities: steps until each pattern dies out
pattern width after 10^6 and 10^7 steps
claims.candidate_data: Direct simulation of totalistic code 1004600 with Wolfram Language or open cellular automaton software.

claims.label: Infinite-time questions about complex systems are almost always undecidable
claims.claim: For almost any system whose behavior seems complex, almost any non-trivial question about its behavior after infinitely many steps (e.g. whether a pattern dies out, becomes repetitive, or ever produces a given arrangement) is undecidable, and such undecidability should be widespread in nature.
claims.quote: for almost any system whose behavior seems to us complex almost any non-trivial question about what the system does after an infinite number of steps will be undecidable.
claims.scope: systems with complex behavior, including simple programs and natural systems
claims.candidate_data: Published undecidability results for cellular automata and tiling problems.

claims.label: Post Correspondence Problem with three pairs is likely undecidable
claims.claim: Whether a set of upper/lower block pairs can be concatenated to give identical strings (the Post Correspondence Problem) is straightforward for two pairs, but already with three pairs there is computational irreducibility, making the question undecidable in general.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that even with just three pairs there is already computational irreducibility
claims.scope: Post Correspondence Problem instances with small numbers of pairs
measurable_quantities: length of minimal solutions for small instances
decidability status for 3-pair instances
claims.candidate_data: Published decidability results for bounded-size Post Correspondence Problem instances and computer searches of small instances.

claims.label: Exhaustive search of 2-state 2-color Turing machines finds three growth rates
claims.claim: Enumerating all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors shows that the maximum number of steps to finish a computation grows with input length only linearly, quadratically, or exponentially, and every exponential case has another such machine computing the same function in bounded steps.
claims.quote: it turns out that the only rates of growth that one ever sees are linear, square and exponential.
claims.scope: all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors, under Wolfram's halting convention
measurable_quantities: maximum steps to halt as a function of input length for each machine
set of functions computed (351)
